01 / A system of agents & factoriesArchitecture study · v0.4

EXOMACHINA.

Independent agents.
Collective intelligence.

A directory of callable capabilities. A catalog of reusable processes. An existing workflow engine brings them together, with explicit ownership, artifact acceptance, and recovery—so agents can compose, maintain, and improve factories as versioned definitions. Every factory has Maintenance & Engineering coverage; proactive research is optional.

02 / Factory Organization

One director.
Three accountable functions.

Production delivers the work. Quality independently checks it. Engineering keeps the factory working and improves its process. Supervisors coordinate specialist workers directly.

04 / An agreed architectural boundary

Coordinate the work.
Encapsulate the worker.

A directory-listed A2A service can fulfill its assignment without knowing the factory graph, adjacent stages, or which service runs next. The factory controls routing and gates, not that service’s internal agents or deployment.

Accepted requirement / factory functionality in the harness

One harness.
Any authorized agent can direct a factory.

The customized Strands harness includes the Factory Module. Each instance is configured as an ordinary agent or a factory; in factory mode, its agent is Director and uses that instance’s normal A2A identity and contract. Callers see the advertised capability, not its internal graph. Factory functionality comes with every harness installation; starting an instance does not start the factory runner unless unfinished factory work needs recovery.

ONE INSTALL / ONE START
Local runtime package

Bundled helpers are allowed.

Start with native local processes. The launcher starts bundled engine and storage helpers only when factory execution or recovery of unfinished factory work needs them. Multiple harness instances may attach to an already-running local runner, with explicit process and store ownership. No separately provisioned workflow platform or Docker prerequisite.

Durable progress and scoped authority

Each instance keeps its identity and state.

Each harness instance owns a stable identity, configuration, workspace and durable state. Restart preserves its work; a new execution incarnation fences stale commands. Quality remains independently authorized through application permissions. Shared infrastructure does not mean shared instance state.

Start simple; defer sandboxing. No sandbox research or implementation until a concrete blocker. The initial trust assumption is trusted local harness code and configured capabilities; state separation is not hostile-code or hard resource isolation. Java/JVM remains a tradeoff to assess through installation, startup/idle footprint and operational burden.

Initially one organization per deployment, with explicit organization ownership and a path to future customers. Kestra remains the earlier behavioral baseline, but its ~650 MiB warm-idle JVM measurement excludes PostgreSQL and Strands, so a separate pair per harness is rejected as the default. Later frozen-graph and original-Task recovery trials make Temporal the conditional development preference, with Effect second and Dagu close third. Kestra’s shared helper and Conductor’s PostgreSQL source variant remain conditional alternatives; the stock Conductor package remains uncleared for this product. Review the bounded spike results ↓

Factory owns cooperation.Versioned steps, dependencies, acceptance gates, budgets, waits, repair bounds, and authority to advance the outer process.
Service owns implementation.Harness, model, provider, reasoning, internal delegation, and fallbacks. The service remains accountable for its promised result.
Platform owns permitted access.Approved identities, discoverable contracts, public guarantees, and invocation permissions. Record the selected binding without exposing private implementation settings.
Enough context to do the job

Task-aware, factory-independent.

Pass the brief, acceptance criteria, permitted artifact references, caller identity, and task context. Opaque correlation IDs are fine. Workers may propose follow-up work; the runtime authorizes changes to the outer process. Engineering deliberately understands factory definitions when authoring or improving them.

Responsibility follows delegation

Hidden collaboration still honors the contract.

Data access, cost, deadlines, cancellation behavior, and independence guarantees apply to internal collaborators too. An independent reviewer must not silently delegate judgment back to the author. The service/platform enforces that guarantee; the factory consumes it.

Message passing can carry artifact references rather than copied payloads. Shared storage does not grant shared authority: each assignment receives only its permitted context.

Proposed authority model

Purpose, process, and execution.

Keep three decisions explicit: why work is authorized, how it advances, and how each assignment is performed.

EXOMACHINA PROPOSAL
Management authorizes work.Own the objective, accountable sponsor, permitted capabilities, spending scope, and escalation destination. Select a published factory version and submit authorized interventions.
The factory governs progress.Own assignments, execution edges, joins, acceptance gates, repair limits, waits, and the authoritative run ledger. Validate commands against the current run before changing its state.
The service fulfills assignments.Own implementation, internal collaborators, private memory, and its remote task state. Report public results and guarantees; expose enough evidence for factory acceptance.

A reporting relationship is not a workflow edge. The same service can participate in several factories. Management views project execution state; they do not become a second scheduler. A request to change a running factory is an authorized command with a recorded outcome. The simple organization has four responsibilities: Director, Production, Quality, and Engineering. They use these same interfaces; the runtime remains the process authority.

Reference patterns: Paperclip accountability ↗ · runtime-enforced review ↗ · worker lifecycle interfaces ↗. The allocation above is an Exomachina proposal.

05 / The missing composition layer

A card gets you discovered.
A contract makes you composable.

Descriptions and media types help discovery. Reliable orchestration also needs explicit inputs, outputs, execution rules, and completion criteria.

Assignment → result

Agree on the shape of the work.

Specify assignment and result schemas, durable artifact references, and completion evidence. Acceptance names the exact artifact revision; a completed task alone does not open a gate.

ILLUSTRATIVE APPLICATION METADATA
Not an A2A core schema or runnable engine definition.

capability: verified-research
contract_version: 1
input:  { brief, source_policy }
output: { report, claims, evidence }
review: { accepted, artifact_revision, findings }
gate: accepted && revision_matches
Bind at execution start.Pin a compatible capability contract, approved service identity, and advertised revision. Record the required public guarantees.
Service administration

Execution profiles live with the service.

Approve harnesses, providers, models, reasoning settings, and internal fallbacks here. A factory selects an advertised capability and public guarantees; it does not configure these implementation details.

Public guarantees

Expose requirements that callers can rely on.

A region restriction or required model may be an advertised service variant or contractual option. Pinning an opaque revision helps traceability; it does not guarantee identical stochastic output. Internal fallbacks must preserve the advertised guarantees.

Persistent service, isolated assignments. Scope conversation and artifacts to the task/context. The source brief defines the requested outcome; the factory ledger records process state and accepted artifact revisions. Attach these policies alongside Agent Cards or through an agreed extension. A2A specification ↗

Other contract dimensions: service binding (identity, revision, public guarantees); context policy (issue fields, artifacts, fresh or continued task); operations (timeout, cancellation, duplicate handling, recovery).

Proposed context model

Knowledge supports work.
Evidence establishes its state.

EXOMACHINA PROPOSAL
Memory is retained knowledge.Preferences, learned facts, and prior experience may help an agent work. Scope retrieval to the assignment’s permissions and relevant provenance; retained memory is not an acceptance receipt.
Skills describe methods.Reusable instructions and procedures help a service execute. They may evolve under service administration without changing the public contract; they do not silently rewrite an active factory version.
The execution ledger records what happened.Assignments, attempts, artifact revisions, decisions, accepted evidence, and authorized transitions establish the run’s state. A conversation summary cannot substitute for that record.

An assignment contains a self-sufficient brief plus permitted references. Continuing a particular task is explicit. Shared service identity does not imply shared conversations or unrestricted memory across factories. The source issue supplies intent; the bound factory version and execution ledger establish process state.

PRIMITIVEREQUIRED MEANINGEDGE CASE TO PROVE
DependencyA prerequisite controls when an assignment may run. Containment and a reference to related work carry no implicit scheduling rule.A support assignment can run while the assignment it helps remains blocked.
Branch & joinRoute on validated values. Each join states required branches, result merge rules, and the meaning of failed, skipped, canceled, or late branches.A canceled branch cannot leave an all-required join waiting forever without an explicit outcome.
Dynamic fan-outGive each discovered work item a stable identity, bounded concurrency, and a defined aggregation rule.Retry or reordered results preserve each item’s lineage and do not create duplicate assignments.
Review & repairReview an exact artifact revision. A repair creates a new revision and consumes an explicit iteration budget.A previous approval cannot release a repaired artifact that has not passed its required gates.
Nested factoryInvoke a published version through its public contract; define context, results, budget attribution, and cancellation propagation.A child may continue remotely after parent cancellation was requested; reconciliation must record the actual outcome.
Durable waitName the awaited event or decision, authorized responder, correlation, expiry, and continuation rule.Duplicate or stale responses cannot advance the same gate twice.

07 / Agents building factories

New compositions.
Controlled publication.

A publication capability gives authoring agents a bounded path from an idea to a reusable factory version.

The factory authoring loop

Author within an approved block profile. Reuse the engine’s schema, validation, definition storage, and execution APIs where available; supply the restricted definition layer when the runtime is code-first.

PROPOSED LIFECYCLE

↺   REVISION LOOP   A validation or test failure returns the definition to Author. Publication requires both gates to pass.

01 / Structural compatibility

Validate assignments, results, artifact references, and the contracts between adjacent tasks.

02 / Authority & scope

Check service identities, public guarantees, context access, side effects, and publication permissions.

03 / Process integrity

Enforce required review gates, bounded loops, and permitted fan-out. Test rejection and recovery paths.

v1 → v2

A new version is a new choice for future runs. Active runs keep their original process binding. Automatic publication can be allowed within policy; exceptions go to an authorized director or human. Human approval is a policy choice.

First agent-authored language: flexible graphs, approved node types. Agents can compose new factories from assignment, typed conditional routing, parallel work with defined joins, bounded loops including review and repair, Director decision waits, and nested published factories; they do not need a preapproved template for each graph. The first profile rejects arbitrary executable expressions, unbounded cycles, unsafe fan-out, and paths that bypass required Quality acceptance or controlled delivery. This profile applies whether the chosen runtime has a native document language or is code-first. New compositions of existing node types publish as documents. Bundled orchestration workers may restart or roll out automatically to load a version, provided each active run retains its exact factory definition, compatible interpreter or worker build, capability contracts, and policy bindings, while external A2A services remain unaffected. A new primitive requires a tested code release.

Proposed authoring workflow

Examples make new factories testable.

AUTHOR → PROVE → PUBLISH
Saved-example development

Exercise a step without repeating the whole run.

Supply representative agent results to test mappings, branches, joins, repair bounds, and rejection paths. Clearly mark substituted data and disable unintended external effects. Separate these authoring tests from evidence that real services recover correctly under concurrent requests.

Learn from completed work

Process engineering turns run evidence into candidates.

Maintenance & Engineering continuously collects accepted artifacts, corrections, and observed decisions to propose improved factory versions. Optional research contributes additional evaluated candidates. Add missing failure paths and permissions, validate the restricted definition, then test and publish a new version. A learned skill or successful trace is source material, not automatic publication authority.

Each release should declare required capability contracts, nested factories, and deployment bindings. Record an immutable definition snapshot or content digest alongside the version label. Existing runs retain their original binding.

08 / Conditional development choice

Temporal leads.
Keep the gates visible.

Compare how the same factory is authored, validated, published, resumed, and inspected. Syntax is only one part of the decision.

Selection gate: a self-contained Strands factory harness within a measured resource envelope. One install/start command may manage bundled local helpers; no separately provisioned workflow service. A warm-idle Kestra JVM measured ~650 MiB RSS before PostgreSQL and Strands; a later shared native-wait bundle measured about 1.3 GB with the Director idle. A separate engine/database pair per harness is rejected, while one shared local helper remains conditional because no whole-install memory ceiling has been agreed. Conductor stock has an uncleared queue dependency; its PostgreSQL source variant remains eligible. Feature scores remain comparison evidence; the 23 September development choice is conditional on these gates. Review the hard-stop audit ↓
CURRENT REASSESSMENT / 23 SEPTEMBER 2026

Choose Temporal for development.

Two fresh independent reviews converged after a frozen four-branch graph test and original-Task crash recovery. This is a development direction, not production qualification. Read the arbitration ↗

01 / TOP PICK

Temporal + stable interpreter

One immutable graph produced repair acceptance and exhaustion; original Director Tasks survived Quality-commit and acceptance-before-release crashes. Ten working A2A calls added 76 MB and no processes in the measured bundle. Exomachina owns the bounded graph language and PostgreSQL lifecycle.

02 / RUNNER-UP

Effect Workflow + Cluster

Fresh graph composition and a smaller local baseline make it the closest fallback. Its product ledger, original-Task recovery matrix, and interpreter-version routing still need proof. MIT v3 packages fit the proposed product path.

03 / CLOSE THIRD

Dagu Community

Native YAML and broader exercised recovery remain valuable. The tested working-A2A path added three processes per assignment; separate-root child coordination and a GPL-compliant bundle remain owned work.

Bounded follow-up, 23 September: typed Director run inputs and a version-pinned interpreter upgrade now pass on ordinary paths. A waiting run stayed on build B1 through B2's publication, and every start named its version explicitly. The one-command package works but is not clean-machine relocatable, and the Temporal frontend is still unauthenticated. The full bundle measured 700–746 MB across 0–10 waiting A2A Tasks, with 40 PIDs. Still open: failed-child and inconsistent-verdict projection to the original Task (unit-tested, unproved live), retiring old builds after drain, contract and policy attestation, online backup and upgrades, and an owner-chosen memory ceiling. Read the integrated verdict ↗ The feature matrix below remains source-coverage evidence, not a replacement for these gates.

Earlier independent review ↗ · Compare DSLs: language quality and agent authoring ↗

HARD-STOP AUDIT / 23 SEPTEMBER 2026

Exclude an exact route, not a whole engine.

A dealbreaker requires a non-negotiable product requirement, primary evidence that a named build or use violates it, and no acceptable path within our constraints. Set resource ceilings before comparing candidates. Both original debate agents and two independent follow-up reviews keep the Conductor source variant and shared Kestra deployment eligible.

EXCLUDED BASELINES

Three routes leave the shortlist.

LangGraph's free first-party production Agent Server route is unavailable under the owner’s no-paid-platform decision; its MIT library would need an owned host. n8n Community does not permit external customers or their agents to author workflow logic. The distributed Windmill Community binary cannot be wrapped or sold as the proposed product without an agreement. Their technical matrix columns remain selectable. Read each scoped exclusion ↓

UNCLEARED ARTIFACT

Hold stock Conductor for product work.

The v3.32.4 server bundle contains an Orkes Community-licensed queue dependency. Its competitive-product restriction leaves both Exomachina development use and distribution rights unresolved; do not use that artifact for either without clearance. A PostgreSQL-only source build removed the dependency and passed a simple workflow/restart trial. Maintaining that source patch and release chain is ongoing work, not a demonstrated inability to use Conductor. Review the source-build evidence ↗

MEASURED COST · NO CEILING

Kestra stays conditional.

The shared native-wait bundle measured 1.285 / 1.287 / 1.301 GB at 0 / 2 / 10 waits, with an idle Director and direct engine starts. Its low incremental wait cost is real; so is its high baseline. JVM tuning and a matched Director-routed comparison remain undone. We rejected one Kestra/PostgreSQL pair per harness, but have not set a whole-install limit that would exclude one shared helper. See the measured topology ↗

OPEN DEVELOPMENT CHALLENGERS

Keep alternatives in view.

Zigflow supplies a declarative Temporal language but lacks a complete A2A factory trial and needs safe worker-version activation. Dagu supplies native YAML; simple native nested approval was demonstrated, but the full typed factory contract on that route remains unproved. The tested typed nested-factory route owns a separate-root recovery bridge. Neither finding is a hard engine exclusion. Read the current ranking ↗

Decision status: Temporal is sufficiently evidenced to start development. The explicit version route and typed Director inputs have ordinary-path passes. Failed-child projection is unproved live, and relocatable packaging plus frontend authentication are unbuilt. Do not eliminate Kestra for RAM without an agreed resource ceiling and a comparable Director-routed measurement; do not eliminate Conductor’s source variant merely for requiring a maintained build. No broad new bakeoff is needed for the development choice.

EARLIER SELECTION REGISTER / 22 SEPTEMBER 2026

Hard stops and open gates come before scores.

Conductor and Kestra led the source-based native-authoring comparison. Dagu, non-development Temporal, core Strands Graph and Effect Workflow + Cluster then received bounded local countertrials. The later common product trials ranked Dagu narrowly ahead of Effect at that stage. The 23 September reassessment now favors Temporal for development, then Effect and Dagu. Argo remains provisional. Three excluded baselines remain visible; all eight historical technical scores are unchanged.

Small native helper.

Durable, with a publication cost.

Strands Graph · pinned trial

Checkpoints need an owner.

Minimal paused Python harnesses measured 71.9 MiB RSS each and resumed pinned graphs after kills. Two unfenced owners of one run both delivered; definition publication, fencing and remote-effect recovery are product work. Evidence ↗

Distributed Community can run ordinary production workers but has proprietary product-use restrictions, quotas and paid performance/governance facilities. How to read the score. Each criterion has a 0–4 burden/proof rating. The weighted contributions total 100. A score of 4 means low owned burden verified on the named release; 2 means material but tractable work; 0 means severe known work that may still be technically possible. Ratings can use observed evidence or an explicit estimate. Unknown is shown as “?” and spans its full possible weight.

PRODUCTION & PRODUCT RIGHTS / SOURCE AUDIT

A free library is not a free production platform.

Review the actual runtime, build and intended use. Internal automation, customer-authored factories and redistributing an engine are different cases. Restrictions below include paid features, runtime dependencies, quotas and gaps in proposed workarounds.

Conductor stock v3.32.4 artifactContains an Orkes Community-licensed queue JAR; rights for this product are not established. A PostgreSQL-only source variant passed a narrow build/restart probe; product packaging and distribution review remain open.

Kestra product packageA host-local one-command bundle passed; clean-machine installation, dependency notices and final distribution remain open.

LangGraph production serverLicense required. Replacing its platform is substantial custom work; the owner’s exclusion stands.

Windmill public OSS buildThe named build enables administrative access without normal authentication. Community authentication is not inherited by compiling public source.

n8n customer-authored factoriesRestricted by the stated free license. A custom UI, agent author or gateway does not change those rights.

BLOCKED means blocked for the named build or use below. It is not a claim that every use of that project is forbidden. Paid permission is not a free workaround. A large replacement subsystem or loss of a required guarantee does not qualify as a small integration.

BLOCKED

The stated use or required facility is unavailable under the assessed terms; no acceptable free path has been established for that condition.

PAID

The named native facility needs a commercial edition; details distinguish feasible alternatives from costly replacements.

LIMIT

A quota, retention bound or execution constraint applies; configurable defaults are identified separately.

CUSTOM

A separately owned component or architecture change is required.

VERIFY

Evidence conflicts or the build/behavior has not been established; do not count it as production clearance.

Windmill13 documented restrictionsOSS auth blocked; CE runs
Production runtime

Community binaries support ordinary production workers. Paid facilities include dedicated warm-script workers and autoscaling. The named public OSS build includes no_auth and resolves requests to an administrative identity; it is not a secure, equivalent replacement.

Open-source product

Non-enterprise source is AGPLv3, with applicable source/notice obligations. Community binaries contain additional proprietary components and cannot simply be redistributed under an OSI license.

Commercial product

AGPL permits commercial use subject to obligations. Distributed Community prohibits selling/wrapping/managed-service use without agreement; internal use and APIs as-is are different.

Activation, renewal & quotas

Enterprise worker source refuses work without a valid license key. Renewal/expiry behavior resides partly in private code and needs contract/build verification. Linux native subworkers are not the same as paid dedicated script workers.

Applies to: Server/client/SSO authentication configuration

Client mode uses caller Kubernetes permissions. Server mode uses the server service account; SSO also needs explicit SSO RBAC to map users to scoped service accounts. Login alone does not establish tenant isolation.

Alternative: Choose client authorization or configure and test SSO RBAC mappings. Retain distinct caller audit evidence and prevent broad server-account access from bypassing the publication boundary.

Workaround assessment: Native configuration path; deployment-specific proof pending

CUSTOM

Name references require immutable publication discipline

Applies to: Template references, active runs and rollout

TemplateRef has no version/digest field. Referenced templates are cached when resolved, so unvisited references may resolve changed names. Secure restriction errors on underlying template changes rather than providing transparent version isolation.

Alternative: Publish dependencies under immutable versioned names, prohibit mutation/deletion while referenced, pin container images and environment bindings, and record the complete dependency set. Test updates during waiting runs.

Workaround assessment: Feasible publication contract; stricter than mutable template updates and unrun

Remote A2A lifecycle and external-effect safety remain integrations

Applies to: Opaque external services and custom HTTP/plugin tasks

HTTP/plugin execution is not native A2A. Persisted engine state, retry nodes and locks do not atomically record an external effect or establish remote stale-attempt fencing after an ambiguous reply.

Alternative: Use a reusable protocol adapter with durable task correlation, service-supported idempotency/status lookup, scoped cancellation and fenced result acceptance. Preserve unknown outcomes when the service cannot prove success or non-execution.

Workaround assessment: Feasible adapter only where remote contracts support it; no universal exactly-once workaround

WHAT REMAINS UNPROVED

This review establishes documented and source-visible restrictions. No candidate has passed a pinned production build or load test. Before selection, record the exact image/source commit, license and feature flags; run without a vendor license or outbound vendor connection where permitted; verify production persistence, restart/recovery, concurrent ownership, throughput and required controls. No native A2A completeness requirement has been added. A reusable adapter remains acceptable. These deployment and licensing gates cannot be waived by a coverage score.

Download the full restriction audit ↗
A2A / AN ACCEPTED INTEGRATION RESPONSIBILITY

Native completeness is not a prerequisite.

A reusable A2A adapter is an acceptable part of Exomachina. Pin the protocol revision and transport, declare the supported subset, and prove task correlation, continuation, artifacts, cancellation and recovery. The engine still owns process transitions; the adapter translates and reconciles remote work.

Do not infer v1 interoperability from an “A2A” label, or assume every implementation is pre-v1. For example, Agent Server documents v1.0 JSON-RPC with missing subscription/push methods. Native support is an integration advantage, not a selection gate. Protocol coverage example ↗

Where an adapter cannot supply the missing guarantee

If a remote action may have succeeded but the service provides neither reliable outcome discovery nor idempotency, no engine can guarantee both eventual retry and zero duplicate effects. Stop unsafe automatic resubmission and preserve an unknown outcome. Similarly, strict remote spend caps require enforceable service limits or trustworthy maximum-cost reservations; stopping new admissions does not stop active remote work.

These are capability-contract constraints, not penalties unique to one engine. A usable workflow can escalate uncertainty; a requirement for fully automatic certainty without those remote guarantees is a real technical blocker. Fault cases E04 and E10 ↗

This is a documented selection assessment, not a runtime pass. Pin the license, distribution, release and required features before adoption. Windmill’s pricing and audit documentation disagree on free audit availability; that remains unresolved rather than an established exclusion. Audit documentation ↗

An earlier independent review
preferred Conductor.

A separate subagent received the product requirements and constraints, with no inherited conversation. It researched primary sources and fixed its provisional choice before reading the existing factual evaluations. It never read the feature score matrix. This source-based review predates the later copied-bundle and Strands/A2A product trials.

Later requirements and source findings qualify this verdict.

The original report below is preserved. Factory functionality must now ship in the Strands harness with automatically managed local dependencies. The reviewed Conductor assembly declares an Orkes Community-licensed queue library; a PostgreSQL-only source variant has since built and passed a simple restart check, but its product package and factory behavior remain unproved. Its proposed ZooKeeper fallback is also unverified in the pinned distribution. Read the new gates and planning evidence ↗

Preferred qualification target

Conductor OSS

v3.32.4

Published factory definitions are runtime data, while independent services complete individually tracked tasks. The reviewer sees this as the closest fit with the least additional authoring-runtime ownership.

CONFIDENCE · MODERATE
Decision boundary

Prove it before adoption.

No candidate has passed every production gate. The recommendation preserves publication without worker refresh and remains conditional on locking, immutable dependencies, customer isolation and recovery races.

NO REQUIREMENTS RELAXED
Overall engine fit and DSL preference are separate judgments.

This earlier source-based review favored Conductor overall, while the separate DSL assessment preferred Kestra’s language. The later product-shaped independent judgment ranked Dagu narrowly ahead of Effect at that stage. The 23 September reassessment now puts Temporal first, Effect second, and Dagu third for development. Neither judgment changes the historical 65-feature source scores; no candidate is production-qualified.

01 / Publication matches the product

New compositions use the existing engine.

Agents can register new arrangements of installed task types through the metadata interface. Factory publication remains separate from deploying capability implementations, so Exomachina does not need to own another workflow interpreter.

02 / Remote assignments stay visible

An outstanding task has an engine identity.

External task completion and persisted gates fit asynchronous services and Director decisions while other branches progress. This is an advantage in task lifecycle design; the reusable A2A adapter still owns correlation and reconciliation.

03 / Custom work stays explicit

Keep the engine responsible for execution.

Exomachina owns catalogs, acceptance, budgets, permissions and remote-service contracts across all candidates. Conductor-specific work centers on a restricted task profile, publication operations and safe lifecycle access. A login proxy alone does not provide customer isolation.

04 / Engineering uses ordinary factories

Recovery and improvement share the runtime.

Engineering can diagnose incidents, perform bounded remediation and propose new versions through workflows. Quality independently evaluates candidates. Optional autoresearch uses the same protected release path. Engine retries alone do not constitute safe self-healing.

Proposed stack / not deployed

Engine, product controls and service adapter.

Build a pinned Apache-licensed OSS server/UI; use PostgreSQL, a restricted publication/authority gateway, an adapter/reconciler and durable object storage. Product records can share PostgreSQL through separate schemas. Operate backups, retention, monitoring and upgrades, and inventory dependencies before redistribution.

Still unqualified / locking + versions

Version labels and database support are not proof.

PostgreSQL locking needs failure and contention tests. Apache ZooKeeper is a documented alternative with extra operating cost. Reject mutation of published definitions and explicitly bind nested factories, capabilities and policies. Engine-unavailable incidents also need an external recovery path.

The strongest objection: reliability after failures.

Conductor’s convenient publication does not prove its lock, retry, callback and cancellation behavior easier to trust than Temporal’s history-based model. The reviewer has not run the proposed Conductor topology. Temporal could win if an acceptable authoring layer passes the publication gate, including an automatically managed, version-pinned worker rollout.

What would overturn or block this recommendation
  1. Immutable publication: publish v2 while v1 waits, alter aliases, restart and resume. Any unapproved dependency drift blocks adoption.
  2. Contested recovery: race completion, timeout, cancellation and recovery owners; lose submission acknowledgements. Reject duplicate effects, stale acceptance and falsely certain outcomes.
  3. Production operation: fail over the database and kill engine/adapter processes during nested waits. Qualify locking, queues, backup recovery and concurrent load.
  4. Product authority: attempt cross-customer access, arbitrary destinations, review bypass and overspending. Required controls must work without paid-only dependencies.
  5. Compare the complete alternatives: prefer Kestra if it needs no more owned coordination and is materially easier to debug. Reconsider Temporal if a maintained, permitted authoring layer passes the same gates.
Read the complete independent review and its primary sources

The reviewer’s complete report follows, including its comparisons, shared responsibilities, licensing distinctions, migration costs, methodology and evidence limits.

My preferred option is Conductor OSS v3.32.4, built from its Apache-2.0 source, with PostgreSQL for persistence, queues, indexing and distributed locks. Confidence: moderate. This is my preferred qualification target, not approval for production adoption. It includes the OSS server/UI, Exomachina’s publication and authority gateway, a reusable remote-service Adapter, and artifact storage. PostgreSQL locking, immutable dependency binding, hostile authoring and recovery races remain adoption gates. No candidate has passed every required gate. The assessed release and license are distinct from Orkes products and their entitlements.

My reason is architectural: Exomachina is principally a product for publishing and executing compositions of independent services. Conductor already treats a process definition as runtime data and external work as individually tracked tasks. That combination offers useful Depth behind an existing Interface without introducing another language interpreter that Exomachina must maintain. I do not propose relaxing the requirement that compositions of existing capabilities publish without worker deployments or refreshes.

Why I prefer this fit. Conductor separates workflow definitions, executions and worker implementations. Definitions contain versioned graphs; the server interprets their ordering and data flow, while workers poll tasks and report results. Its existing metadata publication surface lets an agent or customer submit a new composition of installed task types without changing those workers. This is precisely the separation between factory and capability catalogs that Exomachina needs, although neither engine metadata nor worker registration replaces the product’s public capability contracts. Definition model, execution architecture.

The task lifecycle matters more than the AI integration catalog. A remote research assignment can remain outstanding under a stable engine task identity while other branches progress. A HUMAN task is actually an externally completed gate: an authorized agent Director can complete it as readily as a person. HTTP tasks can also remain IN_PROGRESS after a successful submission using asyncComplete. These are existing continuation mechanisms, rather than a requirement to keep a request open. They still need authenticated correlation and safe completion handling. Human task, released HTTP implementation.

Factories can use native subworkflows internally while exposing the same factory through a public service Interface. Parallel research, synthesis, independent review, bounded repair and a Director decision can remain visible in one engine-owned execution tree. The released subworkflow implementation includes deterministic child identities and cancellation handling. That is source evidence for useful recovery machinery, not proof that every race is safe. Operators, v3.32.4 subworkflow source.

Version numbers are insufficient. Exomachina must reject mutation of published versions, pin every child and capability revision, and preserve policy and execution-profile bindings. Conductor’s mapper retains a workflow definition on the execution but can resolve an unspecified subworkflow version from current metadata. Therefore publication must close over explicit dependencies; dynamic selection must stay inside that approved set. This is a catalog policy over the existing engine, not a second scheduler. Released metadata mapper.

The production path is real and free: shared durable storage, task queues and distributed locking are documented OSS facilities. PostgreSQL can provide all four persistence/queue/index/lock functions, reducing deployment dependencies. The docs explicitly require workload benchmarking, however, and the general deployment guide emphasizes other lock providers. I would qualify the PostgreSQL configuration rather than declare it production-safe from documentation. If necessary, the documented Apache ZooKeeper lock provider is a permitted replacement, at the cost of another operated subsystem. SQLite quickstart success would not settle this. PostgreSQL configuration, production deployment.

What Exomachina actually owns. Across all candidates, the unavoidable work is the public product contract:

  • Separate capability and factory catalogs; schemas, immutable revisions and dependency bindings; authorized publication using the engine’s existing definition language.
  • Acceptance records identifying the exact artifact revision, reviewer independence, repair attempts, and the Director authority that resolved a wait.
  • Admission and atomic budget reservations across concurrent branches; scoped credentials; customer isolation; protected evaluators and publication privileges.
  • A remote-service Adapter preserving task IDs, continuation, artifact references, cancellation and restart reconciliation. Lost acceptance requires service-supported deduplication/discovery or an honest unknown outcome. Engine retries cannot manufacture exactly-once external effects.

I would initially implement these as a small product control Module plus a separately runnable Adapter/reconciler, not one microservice per responsibility. Their durable records can use separate PostgreSQL schemas; artifacts belong in a retained object store. The engine remains responsible for graph transitions, scheduling and execution history. Capability providers retain their private harnesses and models. A new capability implementation can require deployment; rearranging existing capabilities cannot.

Conductor-specific work is narrower: validate an approved JSON task profile, publish through metadata operations, translate task events and expose safe product operations. Customers do not receive unrestricted engine credentials. An OIDC gateway with product authorization, constrained task types and destinations, provider-scoped secrets, and append-only decision records can replace paid identity/governance facilities without importing proprietary code. This is feasible engineering, not an assertion that putting authentication in front of the native UI creates tenant isolation. Operational ownership includes server/database upgrades, backups, retention, monitoring and lock qualification. Source-license permission also does not clear every supplied image: build and inventory a pinned OSS artifact and its dependencies before redistribution.

Temporal is the strongest architectural counterargument. The exact alternative assessed is self-hosted Temporal Server v1.32.0 plus upstream Zigflow v0.15.2, production PostgreSQL persistence/visibility, Temporal UI and retained versioned Zigflow workers. Temporal has the strongest execution-recovery model in this comparison: event history is the recovery mechanism, durable messaging is fundamental, and worker versioning makes long-lived implementation compatibility explicit. Production self-hosting is documented; its MIT core and Zigflow’s Apache core do not require purchasing Cloud. This should carry substantial weight even when a feature checklist favors another engine. Temporal deployment, event history, worker versioning, Temporal license, Zigflow license.

That earlier publication objection is no longer a selection gate. Zigflow compiles and registers definitions when workers start; --watch reloads workers and is documented for development. We now accept automatically managed, immutable worker rollouts when the bundled launcher handles them, active runs keep their exact bindings, and external A2A agents remain untouched. A bounded three-version rollout preserved old runs and left an A2A agent untouched, but an immediate new start once routed to the previous build after set-current-version returned. Publication needs an activation barrier, safe old-worker retirement, and complete one-install validation. Rollout trial ↗ A generic dynamic interpreter can avoid that rollout but makes Exomachina own more of the definition language and its evolution. The additional ownership would be definition semantics, validation, dispatch, publication, immutable binding and interpreter compatibility—not rebuilding Temporal itself. That remains substantially more engine-specific responsibility than a remote protocol Adapter. Zigflow execution model, run command.

Nor should the full Temporal SDK be credited automatically to Zigflow. The local source audit reports nested input/version-binding limitations and sequential runtime iteration despite fixed parallel forks, grounded in the released child invocation and iteration implementations. Those are authoring-layer concerns, not Temporal weaknesses. Temporal’s history debugger and replay discipline would be especially valuable if incident recovery becomes highly interactive; conversely we would operate both Temporal and an independently evolving authoring layer, retain compatible workers, and manage history limits. If publication becomes release-managed by an explicit product decision, I would reconsider Temporal seriously rather than merely move it up a score table.

Kestra OSS v2.0.3 is the closest alternative under unchanged requirements. It has native YAML/API publication, a strong visual authoring and operations surface, revisions, subflows, HTTP integrations and durable pauses. Current documentation explicitly supports distributed HA with the OSS JDBC backend; calling it development-only would be wrong. Its Apache-2.0 core permits a commercial or open-source product, subject to ordinary obligations. Release/license, architecture, HA.

The concrete difference is task completion. Conductor’s external worker/task update protocol makes each remote assignment an addressable outstanding engine task. Kestra can feasibly implement equivalent product behavior with HTTP submission, a subflow containing Pause and typed onResume inputs, bounded status polling, or a reusable custom plugin. Pause explicitly suspends flow scheduling and resumes through an execution operation. Parallel independently waiting assignments therefore need careful subflow organization or plugin behavior. This is additional mapping between service tasks and execution pauses, not missing durable orchestration. Kestra Pause, HTTP Request, Subflow.

The accepted generic A2A Adapter substantially narrows this difference. It needs remote correlation and reconciliation with either engine; Conductor does not eliminate that store or its failure cases. My remaining preference is that its existing task protocol matches the dominant workload directly, with less per-definition ceremony and less reason to maintain an engine plugin. It is a moderate preference. Kestra’s integrated editing/debugging experience could outweigh it if the reference workflow proves equally simple to operate.

Kestra’s native tenant/RBAC/secret integrations are edition-sensitive. A private engine behind the same product gateway, provider-owned secrets and appropriately isolated deployments offers a free permitted path. That limitation also prevents Conductor from claiming an unfair governance advantage. Kestra subflows default to the latest revision, so explicit revision binding is required; its worker/plugin upgrades also need compatibility management. Its richer plugin catalog has more value if Exomachina starts doing substantial work inside the engine, rather than delegating to independently deployed services. Edition comparison, subflow revision semantics.

Argo Workflows v4.1.4 would be compelling with an existing Kubernetes operating team and substantial containerized research or evaluation workloads. WorkflowTemplates provide reusable declarative publication, suspension supports waits, and HTTP templates mean it need not launch a fresh container for every service call. Kubernetes permissions and resource isolation are valuable. Its Apache core is product-compatible. Templates, HTTP templates, license.

For this service-composition product I would avoid making Kubernetes workflow resources the primary authoring abstraction. We would operate the controller/server and cluster, artifact storage and potentially SQL archive/offload, while still implementing service continuation and acceptance policy. Debugging is excellent for workflow nodes and pods but remote task state still needs correlation. Immutable template identities and retained dependencies require publication discipline. Argo is mature and recoverable, not incapable; its operational and conceptual investment pays back best when container execution is central. Archive storage also excludes pod logs unless separately configured. Archive.

Dagu Community v2.17.0 has the most attractive small deployment: a binary, file-backed state, YAML, UI, human tasks and distributed workers. It deserves a real prototype if footprint dominates. Workers communicate status, logs and artifacts through the coordinator, making that coordinator/storage arrangement an important recovery dependency. Its documented automatic DAG retry window also needs explicit treatment for long-lived incidents. Worker deployment, durable execution.

I prefer Conductor’s service/task model and database-backed production operating pattern for the broader product. Dagu can expose factories as independent roots through an Adapter; that is feasible, but cross-root result delivery, cancellation and budgets remain owned coordination. The local screening records this honestly as untested. GPL permits commercial operation and compliant distribution: it is not an internal-use-only restriction. Separately operated Dagu is materially different from distributing a proprietary combined Go binary; the latter is not cleared by its public embedding terms. Community’s paid native SSO/RBAC/audit facilities would require the same external product controls. Licensing, community/paid capabilities.

A later factual cross-check surfaced Tracecat 1.0.1, a maintained Temporal application with dynamic definition publication. It potentially solves Zigflow’s publication problem, but brings a larger application platform and unresolved artifact licensing: its release README excludes both EE code and EE-gating code from the AGPL grant and restricts production/redistribution of those exceptions. I would require an exact permitted free artifact before considering it a replacement. AGPL itself is not the disqualifier. Release terms. LangGraph stays excluded; n8n Community and distributed Windmill Community remain outside this selection. Strands remains a possible worker implementation.

Required Engineering is part of the design. Production, Quality and Engineering can each have one supervisor coordinating workers under the Director. Engineering runs two recurring factory families: incident diagnosis/recovery and continuous improvement. Recovery must reconcile existing remote effects before replacement work, use a fenced recovery owner, retain accepted artifacts, bound repairs and escalate when authority or outcomes are uncertain. Engine retries support this; they do not define safe self-healing. Infrastructure monitoring and database/host recovery also need an external operational path when the engine itself is unavailable.

Improvement consumes incident and quality evidence, proposes a new immutable factory version, runs protected baseline/candidate evaluations, and publishes only through the authorized path. Quality owns acceptance and evaluation; Engineering cannot edit its own passing standard. Optional autoresearch is a bounded candidate generator inside this system, not a substitute for ongoing Engineering. Conductor’s ordinary workflows and external services can express this organization without extra management layers. Every alternative needs essentially the same domain policy; Temporal may handle complicated recovery conversations more elegantly, while Kestra and Argo offer useful experiment operations.

The strongest objection to my choice is ownership after failures. Conductor’s convenient publication does not prove that its current lock, retry, callback and cancellation interactions are easier to trust than Temporal’s history-based model. I have not run the selected Conductor topology. All five candidates have current releases, but release freshness is maintenance evidence, not workload maturity. Temporal’s server maturity does not automatically transfer to Zigflow, and Conductor’s established orchestration design does not automatically qualify newer modules. Conductor’s task definitions and JSON expressions also create migration cost. Keeping service contracts and artifact identities independent helps, but active histories cannot simply migrate to another engine: drain them or maintain the old runtime. The same applies to Temporal/Zigflow, Kestra, Argo and Dagu; an open DSL does not make execution semantics portable.

I would reverse or withhold this recommendation on concrete evidence:

  • Publish two different compositions without refreshing workers; pause v1, publish v2, alter aliases, restart and resume. Any unapproved dependency drift blocks adoption.
  • Race task completion, timeout, cancellation and two recovery owners; lose submission responses and crash after remote acceptance. Duplicate effects, stale acceptance or falsely certain outcomes block adoption.
  • Fail over the database and kill engine/Adapter processes during nested waits and repair. Test lock expiry, queue recovery, backups and realistic concurrent load. PostgreSQL lock failure may change the topology; irreparable engine behavior changes the choice.
  • Attempt cross-customer reads, arbitrary destinations, review bypass and concurrent overspending. The gateway must enforce these without paid-only dependencies.
  • Run identical Engineering/Quality cases on Kestra. If it needs no more owned coordination and is materially easier to debug, prefer it. Reconsider Temporal if a maintained, permitted publication layer passes these tests, or the user explicitly accepts worker lifecycle changes for publication.

Method and evidence: On 2026-09-22 I researched primary documentation, current release metadata, licenses and selected tagged source before reading local evaluations. I fixed the Conductor provisional choice in /tmp/exomachina-independent-first-impression.md; I did not read the ranking matrix. I then checked factual portions of Temporal evaluation, production audit and candidate screening.

The recorded local Temporal probes observed crash recovery without repeating the completed fixture call, failure of a new workflow type before worker refresh, unversioned definition drift, and preservation of old/new results with pinned workers. These are bounded development observations, not my own rerun or production certification. Source findings strengthened the distinction between Temporal and Zigflow; Dagu evidence made its independent-root workaround more credible. Neither changed my provisional choice. Documented capabilities, source-inferred behavior and proposed Exomachina design remain separate from observed runtime proof; all production gates above remain unproven.

Observed / bounded local probes

Recovery worked.
Publication has a condition.

ZIGFLOW 0.15.2 · TEMPORAL SERVER 1.32.0

One run per scenario on macOS arm64, using verified release binaries, Temporal CLI 1.9.1’s SQLite development server and a deterministic localhost HTTP fixture. All test processes were stopped. This establishes specific behavior; production topology, load and A2A interoperability remain untested.

OBSERVED / CRASH RECOVERY

The same run resumed.

Killed both server and worker during a persisted approval wait, then restarted from the same database. After approval, the workflow completed. The fixture observed one HTTP call before the wait and one after. This does not test a lost remote acknowledgement or general exactly-once effects.

OBSERVED / EXPLICIT PINNING

Old run → v1. New run → v2.

Enabled worker versioning, chose pinned behavior, retained the v1 worker and made v2 current. The old waiting run returned 1.0.0; the new run returned 2.0.0. This proves that simple case, not nested factory, service or interpreter-upgrade bindings.

GAP CONFIRMED / NEW FACTORY

A new file needed worker refresh.

Added a definition while the directory worker was running. Its first workflow task failed because the type was unregistered. After refreshing the worker, the pending workflow completed. Stock Zigflow does not satisfy our publication-without-worker-refresh requirement.

GAP CONFIRMED / DEFAULT BINDING

A version label did not freeze the run.

Started a v1 run, replaced its unversioned worker with a changed v2 definition, then approved the wait. The result used v2. Explicit pinning supplies a feasible path; document.version alone does not. This is an unversioned deployment behavior, not a Temporal replay failure.

OBSERVED / VALIDATION

Useful structural rejection.

The representative document passed. Missing taskQueue and an unsupported call failed validation. An extra top-level property was accepted. Validation is therefore useful feedback, not proof that every unknown field or a policy bypass is rejected.

UNRUN / FULL FACTORY CONTRACT

The decisive work is still explicit.

Prove governed publication, nested immutable contracts, safe interpreter upgrades, A2A reconciliation, concurrent duplicate handling, exact-revision acceptance, budgets and Engineering recovery. The small probes do not mark E01–E10 complete.

Released DSL limitations beyond the publication gate
  1. Do not inherit the entire Temporal SDK matrix. In Zigflow 0.15.2, runtime for loops are sequential; static fork branches do not supply a bounded runtime-sized parallel map.
  2. Nested version selection needs work. The inspected run.workflow call uses the child type name; declared namespace/version are not an immutable dependency binding. Listener routing follows the actual workflow execution, so signaling a parent does not automatically reach a listener inside its child.
  3. acceptIf is not an authorization or stale-command validator. The inspected Update handler stores data before checking completion, and its Temporal validator returns success. Enforce director authority and revision checks at the appropriate boundary.
  4. Released cancellation differs from current main. A stronger fork cancellation change that waits for child closure was not in the pinned release. A separate listen.any completion concern came from source inspection and remains unreproduced.
  5. Restrict what definitions may execute. Script/container/HTTP/activity facilities and inherited environment are authority surfaces. An authoring schema alone is not a sandbox or a publication policy.

These are pinned-source findings, separate from the five observed probe groups. Exact locations, feasible paths and remaining uncertainty are in the machine-readable evaluation.

Current recommendation: keep Temporal in the direct comparison.

Conductor and Kestra still offer the more direct native publication path. Temporal may be preferable if a maintained authoring layer or a deliberately restricted interpreter keeps ownership acceptable and its runtime strengths reduce total work. Stock Zigflow is promising, but has not cleared that publication gate. No custom DSL or rollout-based publication model has been adopted.

Nested decisions / two native mechanisms

Two different wait mechanisms.

The typed, processless human.task action is root-only. Native sub-DAG approval/resume also exists. Evaluate the simpler native approval path first; it is not automatically equivalent to typed input, released waiting capacity or proven crash recovery.

Human-task persistence, completion, and root-only restrictions ↗Approval gates and review semantics ↗Sub-DAG approval and resume implementation ↗

PAID Community controls: first administrator and at most two API keys; additional user management, OIDC/SSO, administrative audit logs and incident routing require paid controls. A private engine behind a tested Exomachina authorization and audit layer is a possible alternative, not native feature parity. Edition limits ↗

Separate root factories: plausible, not proven.

Yes, provisionally: expose every reusable factory as an independent root run behind an HTTP service, optionally with an A2A facade. Each root may then own processless waits. Dagu's scheduler still owns queueing and execution; Exomachina needs a durable service-coordination adapter, not a replacement DAG scheduler.

Correlate immutable factory versions and logical invocations; reconcile early or lost callbacks, concurrent submissions, cancellation, deadlines and shared budgets. Each root keeps Dagu as its scheduler. The adapter cannot depend on an in-memory parent/child map.

All seven focused restrictions and possible alternatives
BLOCKED

GPL obligations for a combined distribution

The public source license is GPL-3.0-or-later. Proprietary distribution that links the experimental Go API raises combined-work obligations; the vendor offers separately negotiated non-GPL embedding rights.

Blocking condition: Blocking only if our chosen distribution forms an incompatible combined work and we require neither GPL compliance nor a separate agreement.

Alternative to assess: Evaluate a separate server/HTTP packaging model and its actual notices/source delivery. Do not infer that a container boundary settles every licensing question. Commercial customer-authored workflows are not themselves prohibited by GPL.

Dagu GPL license ↗Dagu embedding and GPL licensing guidance ↗
PAID

Community identities and paid controls

Community supports the first administrator and up to two API keys. Additional user management, OIDC/SSO, audit logs, and incident routing are paid controls. Workspace roles are explicitly not tenant isolation.

Alternative to assess: A private runtime behind Exomachina-owned authentication, authorization, audit, and per-tenant deployment boundaries is feasible engineering. It must not expose an unrestricted engine credential to customers. This does not make native Community RBAC or audit complete.

Self-hosted license comparison ↗Builtin authentication, licensed controls, and workspace limits ↗
PAID

Activation for optional paid controls

With no configured license, source enters Community mode without activation. Key-based paid activation uses periodic heartbeats; signed inline/file JWT sources do not. License startup failures degrade rather than block application startup.

Alternative to assess: Do not describe Community as requiring registration or payment. If paid controls are chosen, establish supported offline entitlement and failure behavior for those controls. This inspection does not certify absence of every unrelated outbound request.

Community startup and paid activation manager ↗License sources and heartbeat applicability ↗
LIMIT

Root-only typed human tasks

The processless typed action human.task is allowed only in roots, not DAGs invoked by dag.run, dag.enqueue, or parallel. It also rejects foreach placement and step timeout settings.

Alternative to assess: Evaluate independent root services for reusable factories. Do not generalize this restriction to every approval gate: current source has sub-DAG approval/resume endpoints, while approval inputs differ from typed human-task outputs.

Human-task persistence, completion, and root-only restrictions ↗Approval gates and review semantics ↗Sub-DAG approval and resume implementation ↗
VERIFY

Retry eligibility and recovery window

Automatic DAG retries require the scheduler, explicit retry policy, and an eligible failed top-level run. The default scan window is 24 hours from the original run timestamp, so long-lived runs can age out.

Alternative to assess: Configure the recovery window for factory lifetimes and define escalation beyond it. Worker-crash tests in source demonstrate failure detection paths, not verified exactly-once external effects or complete Exomachina recovery.

Automatic retries and scheduler recovery window ↗Worker-crash and distributed recovery integration tests, inspected only ↗
CUSTOM

Durable relationships between separate roots

HTTP-started roots are not automatically a native parent/child execution tree. Dagu can own each root's execution while Exomachina owns the logical service relationship.

Alternative to assess: Persist versioned invocation identity, parent/child linkage, deadline and budget authority, cancellation state, accepted results, and recovery ownership. A one-shot callback or in-memory map is insufficient.

Dagu REST API, root execution, and completion endpoints ↗Root submission, supplied run IDs, and start timeout behavior ↗Human-task persistence, completion, and root-only restrictions ↗
CUSTOM

Transport configuration

Distributed transport documents TLS/mTLS, but peer.insecure defaults to true. Web/API TLS is a separate concern. No paid-only transport gate was identified in the reviewed Dagu documentation.

Alternative to assess: Configure and test authenticated encrypted transport plus private API access. Do not equate available TLS with a hardened default installation.

Distributed TLS and mTLS configuration ↗
Eight proof obligations / all unrun
  1. D01 / Pin a distributable production baseline

    Build/deploy the chosen released artifact without registration or a paid key; document separate-service versus combined-binary packaging.

    Pass evidence: Required capabilities exist in that release; GPL notices/source delivery and product license boundaries are resolved; no trial expiry governs the Community runtime.

  2. D02 / Both roots wait across complete host loss

    Caller and callee independently reach durable checkpoints; kill server/scheduler/workers, replace workers, edit the source definitions, then complete the waits.

    Pass evidence: Waits free execution capacity, persist through restart, resume the intended snapshots, and produce one accepted downstream effect.

  3. D03 / Lost acceptance and duplicate submissions

    Drop the child-start response after acceptance and concurrently retry the same logical invocation from two recovery processes.

    Pass evidence: One logical child and one external effect; existing execution is recovered rather than duplicated. Run-ID prechecks alone are not accepted as concurrency proof.

  4. D04 / Early, duplicated, stale, and partially committed results

    Deliver a child result before the caller checkpoint, duplicate it, lose the resume response, and fail queueing after completion was persisted.

    Pass evidence: Durable reconciliation eventually resumes once; incompatible or revoked results cannot overwrite accepted state; no completed input is lost.

  5. D05 / Cancel and expire a waiting tree

    Cancel/expire the caller while the child is running or waiting, including a race with result delivery and recovery-owner replacement.

    Pass evidence: Cancellation/deadline policy reaches every correlated root and remote assignment; no late callback resurrects authority or permits a new effect.

  6. D06 / Concurrent budgets and isolation

    Fan out competing independent roots under one budget, then crash the reservation owner; attempt cross-customer API and artifact access.

    Pass evidence: Atomic reservations cap aggregate use, recovery reconciles outstanding spend, and the Exomachina gateway/deployment boundary enforces tenant access despite shared engine credentials.

  7. D07 / Long-lived failure recovery and worker leases

    Kill workers during a remote side effect, test coordinator replacement, and fail a run older than the configured automatic-retry window.

    Pass evidence: One fenced recovery owner reconciles effects before replay; failure beyond the window is escalated or explicitly recovered without silent abandonment.

  8. D08 / Compare native sub-DAG approval with root-service composition

    Run a nested approval gate locally and on distributed workers; approve, reject, restart, and lose a response.

    Pass evidence: Determine which requirements native approval meets, including release of waiting capacity and parent continuation; add an adapter only for the remaining typed-wait/service semantics.

Promotion rule: Keep Dagu under evaluation and run the bounded root-service/recovery spike. Promote only if GPL packaging fits, Community controls can be contained by an acceptable product boundary, and the durable integration remains smaller than the infrastructure it replaces. Do not assign a weighted feature score yet.

Current documentation and repository main can precede a released binary. Pin a release and confirm every relied-on capability before the spike.

Other references and architectural alternatives

Effect Workflow + Cluster is the 23 September development runner-up, though it remains unscored in the historical source-coverage matrix. Its MIT-licensed v3 packages offer durable activities, retries, timers, external waits and a SQL-backed single-node runner. A pinned SQLite-backed Node helper resumed a paused wait after a process kill; that narrow trial measured about 185 MiB warm-idle RSS for the helper alone. One-install packaging, the full Strands-plus-helper footprint, multi-harness operation and broader recovery remain open. The documented workflow definitions are TypeScript code. For agents to publish factory documents without deploying new code, Exomachina would need to own the restricted document format, validation, catalog and immutable version binding. Effect v4 is currently a release candidate, and its cluster and workflow modules are marked unstable. Temporal is the conditional first development choice.

Hatchet (Go, MIT) is a potentially strong runtime substrate, but its workflows are defined in SDK code rather than a native factory-document language. Its new Python embedded mode starts a local sidecar with bundled PostgreSQL and no Docker. Hatchet documents that mode for local development and CI; production packaging, lifecycle, footprint and multiple harnesses remain to be proved. Agent-authored factory documents would require an Exomachina-owned interpreter and publication path.

Restate (Rust) is another potentially strong durable substrate, with a local server binary and code-defined Python handlers. Its BUSL-1.1 license is not open source today. The grant explicitly permits a public workflow product built through a GUI, DSL or proprietary API when consumers do not directly use Restate APIs to specify, add or invoke workflows; it prohibits a managed service where third parties register their own Restate service endpoints and invoke them. The product boundary and a document interpreter remain selection gates. Fabro merits a focused check of its single-server, early-access deployment constraints. These are unscored references, not overall recommendations. Symphony, Paperclip, Hermes, and Grok Bot still inform work management, ownership, recovery and learning; they do not add a second scheduler.
