What A2A buys us

A shared interface for remote work.

Agent Cards advertise capabilities and endpoints. Messages, task/context IDs, statuses, artifacts, and cancellation requests give the adapter a common vocabulary. Input-required and auth-required states support interrupted interactions. Streaming or push updates can reduce polling when supported.

Protocol specification ↗ · Asynchronous operations ↗

What Exomachina must decide

Process meaning and operational guarantees.

Factory versions, dependencies, service selection, review gates, repair limits, budgets, and board semantics belong to our orchestration design. A2A does not choose the next factory stage or establish that a returned artifact meets our acceptance criteria.

Our architectural allocation: the protocol is the adapter’s shared language; the workflow engine remains the process authority.

Completion ≠ acceptance

A remote task can finish while its result still fails factory review. Validate the result before advancing a gate. A terminal A2A task cannot restart; a refinement begins a new task, potentially within the same context. Task lifecycle ↗

Correlation ≠ deduplication

The current spec makes Send Message idempotency optional; a message ID alone is not an exactly-once guarantee. Define and test concurrent duplicate handling. A cancellation request also needs a reconciled outcome. Idempotency semantics ↗

STATE → VIEW

A board is an operational view of the factory. Project assignments, waits, gates, and attempt history from authoritative execution records. Route operator commands through the same lifecycle rules. Prefer engine facilities and a small integration layer over a second independently authoritative scheduler.

Design agenda / resolve before calling recovery complete

01 / Identity & ownership. Define assignment-to-attempt-to-remote-task mappings, retention, and how a stale attempt loses authority to commit a result.

02 / Submission ambiguity. Persist intent and correlation; handle a lost response after remote acceptance. Test concurrent submissions and recovery after a crash before the remote ID is recorded.

03 / State reconciliation. Map remote states to workflow waits and gates. Reconcile duplicated, delayed, or reordered updates against the service’s current task state.

04 / Recovery & side effects. Separate reconnect, retry, repair, and cancellation. Bound retries, define deadlines and compensation where needed, and verify service guarantees under concurrency.

05 / Evidence & operator actions. Define accepted artifact storage, board projections, audit history, and authorized unblock/cancel commands without creating competing state owners.

06 / Engine proof. Kestra has passed bounded native restart, publication, harness and A2A/acceptance probes. A host-local bundle passed one-command restart; clean-machine installation and product rights review remain open. Conductor’s stock artifact remains uncleared; a later PostgreSQL-only source build passed a simple workflow/restart but has not run the factory slices. Argo, Temporal and lighter options remain conditional comparisons if Kestra fails its remaining gates. Keep excluded LangGraph, n8n and Windmill visible for technical comparison. Measure what the engine supplies and what the adapter must add.

Proposed evidence modelFOUR DISTINCT FACTS
PRODUCEDResult exists
→
STOREDDurable revision
→
DELIVERED TO REVIEWERReview input received
→
ACCEPTEDGate evidence

Preserve before cleanupA declared output must be durably stored and readable by its authorized consumer before its temporary workspace is reclaimed.

Approve the exact revisionBind acceptance to artifact revision, verification policy, reviewer identity, and evidence. Repair or changed source evidence triggers the declared downstream invalidation rules.

Recover the failed stageA failed reviewer handoff does not imply that artifact production failed. Retain the stored revision and handoff receipt. Consumer publication has its own sequence: accepted revision → authorized publication → delivery to the consumer.

Proposed artifact review milestones, not an A2A state machine. Delivery here means delivery to the reviewer; it does not authorize public release. References: Hermes durable artifacts ↗ · separate execution and delivery outcomes ↗ · decisions tied to target state ↗.

Proposed recovery contract

Unknown is an outcome to reconcile.

A lost response may follow remote acceptance. It does not establish that work failed to start.

DESIGN TO PROVE
Submission and observation

Persist intent before dispatch.

Record the assignment, attempt, selected service, submission identity, and side-effect policy. Reconnect to known work after transport failure. If acceptance is ambiguous, query by the supported identity or use the service’s tested duplicate-handling contract. Escalate when neither can resolve the outcome.

Authority and recovery

One current attempt may advance the gate.

A reclaimed attempt loses authority to commit an accepted result even if it finishes late. Classify temporary service failures, invalid configuration, rejected artifacts, legitimate waits, and repeated unsuccessful recovery separately. Every retry has a reason and a bound.

Execution durability, result durability, and delivery durability are separate properties. A durable completion receipt cannot restart a lost worker. A live connection or process does not prove progress. Admission limits prevent new starts; cancellation of existing work requires its own observed result.

Reference patterns: Paperclip run ownership ↗ · Hermes failure classification ↗ · completion delivery durability ↗. Local atomic claims do not establish exactly-once remote effects.

Proposed operating policy

Bound work before it expands.

CONTROL + OBSERVATION
Attribute costs to the work.Track organization, factory-run, and assignment spend. Keep unknown prices visible. A strict spending ceiling needs service participation and reservations that account for concurrent in-flight work; delayed usage reports alone cannot enforce it.
Reconcile before admitting more.Resolve existing assignments and stale ownership before new dispatch. Apply shared capacity and per-capability limits. Distinguish pausing new starts from canceling active work, and make manual overrides auditable.
Coalesce triggers deliberately.Define whether overlapping starts queue, merge, or skip, and bound catch-up after an outage. Wake agents for work or required decisions. Repeated identical incidents should retain history without flooding operators.

Reference patterns: Paperclip usage attribution ↗ · coalescing and catch-up ↗ · Hermes pause semantics ↗. Strict budget and concurrency guarantees require proof against the chosen engine and services.

10 / Maintain, improve, explore

A factory that recovers.
A process that improves.

Engineering owns required maintenance and continuous improvement. Quality independently evaluates its changes. Optional autoresearch explores better ways to operate within the same simple organization.

REQUIRED FACTORY CAPABILITY

Name the owner, health signals, permitted remedies, improvement objectives, budgets, and escalation route. Observe events continuously and review outcomes on a bounded schedule. These responsibilities run alongside production; completed factory runs can finish normally.

Engineering owns these operating loops within the Factory Organization. Production carries out the work; Quality independently evaluates outputs and proposed changes.

Three operating loops

Choose the reason for change.

Trigger / degraded or interrupted operation

Restore the promised behavior.

Ordinary retries remain engine behavior. Escalate recurring, unknown, or policy-significant failures into one owned incident with retained evidence.

  1. 01Detect & claimDeduplicate the incident; one current recovery owner.
  2. 02ReconcileInspect attempts, remote state, and accepted artifacts.
  3. 03RemediateRun a permitted recovery playbook within its bound.
  4. 04VerifyObserve restored health and contract compliance.
  5. 05Close or escalateRetain the incident outcome and prevention findings.
Authority: the current operating policy.

Reconnect, resume, restart a permitted worker, or use an already approved fallback. A change to factory logic or a service revision enters the candidate-release path. Repeated failed recovery opens the escalation route.

Trigger / accumulated operating evidence

Turn experience into a better version.

Continuously collect traces and periodically compare outcomes. Recurring repairs, successful shortcuts, quality regressions, and high-cost steps feed process engineering.

  1. 01ObserveBind evidence to the actual factory and service versions.
  2. 02ProposeExplain a change and its expected improvement.
  3. 03EvaluateCheck contracts, held-out quality, cost, and uncertainty.
  4. 04PromotePublish an eligible new version through the release gate.
  5. 05Observe againMeasure rollout; retain or roll back future admission.
Authority: the shared publication policy.

Store unsuccessful edits and their evaluation context so future proposals can learn from them. Active runs retain their bindings. Service-internal changes remain service-owned releases.

Trigger / an enabled research campaign

Search before there is an incident.

A charter defines the objective, fixed evaluator, editable surface, reference environment, trial limits, aggregate budget, and stopping conditions.

Preview: no research trials are admitted. Maintenance and continuous improvement remain active.

  1. 01Measure baselineRecord an unchanged, reproducible starting point.
  2. 02Form hypothesisChange only the surface allowed by the charter.
  3. 03Run bounded trialAccount for execution, evaluation, and model costs.
  4. 04Keep or discardRecord valid, failed, and inconclusive results.
  5. 05Offer candidateA promising trial enters the same publication gate.
Keeping a trial selects the experimental incumbent.

Production promotion is a separate decision. Disabling research stops new trials; an active trial follows its declared finish-or-cancel rule. A campaign stops on budget, deadline, cancellation, or its declared search limit.

One route for lasting changes

Candidate → evidence → policy → new version

Check semantic invariants before comparing quality and cost. Enforce capability permissions, required review, artifact revision checks, and bounded work. Pin the evaluator, data, candidate, and environment; Quality independently records results. A crash or invalid metric cannot become a winning score.

Automatic within declared scope. An authorized release capability can promote passing changes without a human at every step. Exceptions route to the director.

One current version transition. Concurrent promotions check the expected incumbent. A stale candidate must be re-evaluated or handled by an explicit policy.

Observe, then retain or roll back. Control future admissions, retain release history, and preserve active-run evidence. Recovery requiring a new version transfers authority to explicitly linked successor work. Fence the old run and reconcile outstanding action identities before any repeated effect.

When the caretaker fails

Recovery has its own failure contract.

Persist incident ownership and reject stale recovery commands. A small independent platform watcher can perform bounded engine or Engineering-service restarts and escalate when the main runtime is unavailable. It does not reschedule factory assignments. Recovery cannot rely solely on the failed recovery owner.

A protected improvement boundary

The experimenter cannot rewrite its judge.

Keep evaluation, permissions, budgets, and promotion rules outside the editable experiment surface. Changes to protected authority or evaluation policy require an independently controlled release. All engineering evaluations use separate credential scopes and protected production/recovery capacity. Optional research adds its own campaign admission limits.

Research influences / applied to our architecture

Learn from traces. Test the change.

NO NEW UNIVERSAL WORKFLOW LANGUAGE
Procedural Graphs

Local guidance and evaluated edits.

The paper combines step-local procedural advice with separately evaluated graph changes. Exomachina can use advisory procedures inside a service and trace-derived proposals for factory definitions. The engine continues to enforce gates. Compare ordinary skills, raw local context, and generated guidance before adding model calls.

Borrow the measured baseline, narrow editable surface, fixed trial budget, and keep/discard history. Adapt the pattern to factory definitions or service-owned changes under a research charter. Exomachina adds campaign limits, independent evaluation, production isolation, and governed release.

How the ranking is calculated

Importance: Most × 5 · Mid × 3 · Least × 1.
Support: ● Full × 1 · ◐ Partial × 0.5 · ○ None × 0.

SCORE = 100 × Σ(IMPORTANCE × SUPPORT) / 247

33 Most + 25 Mid + 7 Least = 247 available points. All 65 rows count once, including Next and Optional; those statuses add no second weight. Partial support receives half credit as a comparison convention, not a measurement of implementation effort.

These weights are an explicit recommendation for this architecture. They give Most features five times the influence of Least features. Bars split earned points into Most, Mid and Least contributions.

Scores describe documented coverage in each stated baseline. They do not measure quality, cost, reliability or runtime performance. A critical missing guarantee remains a blocker regardless of total. Paid, preview and limited capabilities retain their partial ratings.

Coverage ranks use all eight options and stay fixed when you filter features or select columns. Cards are numbered within the non-excluded outer-runtime pool; option chips retain the overall rank. Recommendation roles are independent. Dagu is not scored. Ties use Most coverage, then Mid coverage, then alphabetical display order; an exact score tie is not a meaningful preference. Baselines, editions and scope for selected options
Conductor

Self-hosted Conductor OSS with documented free integration modules enabled. Current official documentation assessed 2026-09-21; no release pinned or runtime conformance tested. Enterprise-only capabilities are partial, not baseline support.

Windmill

Self-hosted distributed Windmill Community Edition, with OpenFlow, official APIs and Workflow SDKs. These binaries include proprietary components under additional terms; they are not a purely open-source baseline. A non-enterprise AGPLv3 source build is a separate option: the audited oss feature set enables no_auth and cannot inherit Community authentication or RBAC claims. Capability documentation assessed 2026-09-21; license distinction verified 2026-09-22. No runtime-tested or pinned release. Paid-only and beta capabilities remain partial; HTTP/MCP do not imply native A2A.

Kestra

Self-hosted Kestra OSS with free public core/AI plugins. Current official documentation assessed 2026-09-21; no release pinned or runtime conformance tested. Enterprise/Cloud-only capabilities are partial, not baseline support.

Argo Workflows

Self-hosted Apache Argo Workflows OSS on Kubernetes, including the standard controller/server, HTTP templates, optional approved executor plugins, configured artifact storage and optional SQL persistence. Current official documentation and source snapshot 8a6f33f90a2124878db858e04c6999d3c5ab63b2 assessed 2026-09-22; no pinned release deployment or runtime conformance tested. Argo CD, Argo Rollouts and bespoke A2A/domain services are not credited as native Workflows features.

Temporal

Self-hosted open-source Temporal Server with official SDKs and Web UI; current documentation assessed 2026-09-21. Normal Workflow SDK code counts for generic orchestration. Preview features remain partial; no runtime certification.

n8n

Self-hosted n8n Community, including optional free registration and public built-in integrations. Source-available rather than OSI open source; paid Business/Enterprise features excluded. Current documentation assessed 2026-09-21; preview features partial.

Strands

Self-hosted open-source Strands Agents/Harness SDK Graph and workflow composition in Python and TypeScript, including the official Python community workflow tool and Python Strands Evals companion where explicitly noted. SDK capabilities differ by language; neither language uniformly inherits the other’s features. Hosted AgentCore services and deployment control-plane guarantees are excluded. Current official documentation and repository main sources assessed 2026-09-21; no release pinned or runtime conformance tested.

LangGraph

Open-source Python LangGraph with official persistent checkpointers/stores and synchronous checkpoint durability configured for production. Current official docs assessed 2026-09-21, including documented 1.2 APIs; no release pinned or runtime conformance tested. LangSmith Agent Server, Studio, evaluation and Engine features are outside this OSS baseline and receive at most partial support. Ordinary SDK graph code counts for general execution; bespoke factory subsystems do not.

Scope update: these scores retain the earlier engine capability assessment. Self-contained factory operation in the Strands harness is now required. Local packaging, the ~650 MiB warm-idle Kestra JVM and the Conductor dependency restriction are selection gates, not extra points silently folded into these totals. 12 / The implementation frontier

Small custom surface.
Clear responsibilities.

Adopt the engine’s workflow machinery. Build the catalog bindings, capability contracts, publication policy, and maintenance authority specific to Exomachina.

Observed S0–S4 / 22 September 2026

The behavior works.
The footprint decides.

The approved, narrowed first round ran in parallel with related fixtures. Conductor stopped at its stock artifact gate in the first round; a later PostgreSQL-only source variant passed a narrow workflow/restart check. Kestra ran the native workflow, harness, publication and recovery probes. Kestra is the observed behavioral baseline. Per-harness Kestra is rejected as the default; a shared-local package remains conditional. No product engine was committed at that stage; no option is production-qualified yet.

Accepted / deployment experience

One install.
One start command.

Each customized Strands harness instance is configured as an ordinary agent or a factory. In factory mode, its agent is Director behind the instance’s normal A2A contract. The bundled local runner starts on factory use or recovery of unfinished work; other harness instances may share that runner. No separately provisioned workflow service is required.

ONE ORGANIZATION INITIALLY
Observed selection gate

Qualify the actual package.

Conductor’s stock v3.32.4 server contains an Orkes Community-licensed queue dependency and is not cleared for this product. A source variant without that direct dependency built and restarted a simple PostgreSQL workflow; its product package and S1–S4 remain open. A host-local Kestra bundle started JDK, PostgreSQL and engine together; ~650 MiB warm-idle JVM RSS makes a separate pair per harness too heavy as the default. Shared-local footprint, clean-machine install and distribution rights remain open.

FEATURE RANK ≠ PRODUCT ELIGIBILITY

Accepted simplification: stable identity and durable state for every instance; native processes first. Sandboxing is deferred until a concrete blocker and is outside these spikes. Java/JVM remains eligible only if the complete shared-local package fits the agreed footprint and operating burden.

S0 / conditional

Actual runtime package

Conductor’s stock artifact is uncleared, while its PostgreSQL-only source variant passed a separate narrow restart probe. Kestra with JDK 25 and PostgreSQL survived stop/restart; a copied macOS arm64 bundle repeated it with one start command. Clean-machine installation, notices and total memory with two harnesses are open.

S1 / narrow pass

Contested engine state

Eight simultaneous resumes made one downstream run. Five resume/kill races ended in stable terminal states, each with at most one downstream run. Single-server, no external effect.

S2 / one native wait passed

A harness becomes a factory

One Strands package ran capability and Director roles. A Kestra-backed Director survived two restarts; eight repeated starts and decisions yielded one native run and downstream task. Native child work remains unproved.

S3 / binding mechanics passed

Native definitions and fixed bindings

Kestra ran a synthetic parallel/repair/Director-wait YAML fixture. Explicit child revision pinning held; unpinned lookup changed to v2. A schema-valid review bypass also published, so complete policy enforcement is open.

S4 / selected windows pass

Remote work and acceptance

Kestra called a live Strands A2A service, then a product ledger accepted the exact artifact and recovered continuation after exits. Async tasks and lost engine-to-A2A receipt remain unproved.

S5 / deferred

Budgets, repair and improvement

Required Engineering and optional autoresearch remain in the architecture. Their full authority, budget, rollout and quality qualification belong to the next development phase.

S6 / bounded round two

Six runtime countertrials.

Dagu, Strands Graph, Effect, Temporal, Restate and Hatchet now have pinned local v1/v2 trials. Stable interpreters removed the worker-rollout concern in narrow fixtures. Complete Strands/A2A, artifact acceptance, offline packaging and matched resource qualification remain open; the broad S6 scenarios are still deferred.

After engine choice / before production claims

Qualify the complete product

Real agents and protocol compatibility; all required Engineering cases; actual load, backups and upgrades. Optional research and future shared-customer operation have separate activation gates.

Historical decision-round result: Dagu narrowly led Effect. That development order is superseded by the 23 September reassessment.

The common Strands/A2A decision-round trials put native Dagu YAML ahead on agent-authored factory definitions, while Effect leads on tested acceptance replay. Both copied local bundles relaunched after a hard stop with two A2A factory tasks waiting. Dagu requires host-unique run IDs and a GPL-compliant release bundle; neither candidate has passed full production qualification.

The custom-work assumption is itself under test. A small harness Interface must hide the difficult integration. If it grows into a second scheduler, universal interpreter or substantial engine fork, reconsider the design.

Planning baseline · 22 September 2026 · The owner approved a narrowed S0–S4 round, executed in parallel with isolated environments. Read the observed results and remaining gates before using this original plan. S5 and the broad S6 comparison remain deferred. Source inspection is evidence for a hypothesis, not an experimental result.

Recommendation

The deployment gate is settled: one install/start command must supply factory functionality without a separately provisioned external workflow service. Automatically managed bundled local helper processes are allowed. The earlier required shared-Conductor-server assumption is superseded. Existing engine rankings describe the prior operating model and do not clear this new gate.

The original plan proposed seven bounded spikes, S0–S6, around one reusable reference factory. The approved first round narrowed this to the package gate, contested-state litmus, harness, native publication and remote recovery. Conductor-specific runtime work stopped at its stock artifact's unresolved license gate; Kestra cleared a local behavioral screen and was used for the bounded runtime probes. Its one-install product package remains unproved.

Passing these spikes would support an engine decision and implementation of the first product slice. It would not qualify a production deployment. Full E01–E10, M01–M08 and applicable R01–R05 scenarios remain the broader acceptance plan; a narrow probe does not mark a whole scenario passed. The existing Temporal/Zigflow probes remain valid for their recorded scope and need not be repeated.

The largest architecture risk is the assumption that a native workflow engine plus a small custom Module can enforce publication, remote recovery, exact-revision acceptance and Director authority. The spikes must measure that owned complexity, as well as whether the engine runs.

Decisions and the updated harness architecture
  • Accepted: initially one organization per deployment, preserving a path to multiple customers. Organization ownership belongs in durable records and public Interfaces. Shared-engine customer isolation is a future qualification; role authorization and scoped credentials are required initially.
  • Accepted: factory functionality is built into the customized Strands harness. Any appropriately configured agent using that harness can operate as a factory service. Its agent acts as the factory Director. A separate factory-service application per agent is not required.
  • Accepted: the harness cannot require an externally provisioned orchestration service. One install/start command supplies factory operation and can automatically manage bundled local engine/storage helper processes. Agents should readily expose A2A factory endpoints. An in-process-only engine is not required; a separately managed shared server is not the baseline. Reuse of one locally managed engine across agents in an installation is a design option to evaluate, rather than launching an engine/database per agent by default.
  • Accepted: every harness instance has its own stable identity and durable state, regardless of any future sandbox choice. Scope configuration, workspaces, artifacts and pending work by instance; restarting an instance preserves its identity and state while replacing its execution incarnation. Logical ownership does not require a separate database or engine process for every instance.
  • Accepted simplification: start with native local processes and defer sandboxing until a concrete blocker warrants it. No sandbox comparison, implementation or whole-harness containment proof belongs in the initial spikes. Docker is not a baseline prerequisite; optional isolation must not drive the first design.
  • Evaluation preference: Java/JVM is a deployment tradeoff, not an exclusion. Judge the actual installation, startup and idle footprint, helper lifecycle and upgrade burden. Do not introduce a replacement runtime or custom scheduler merely to avoid a language.
  • Preserved: native factory definitions; publication of new compositions without harness/worker refresh; independent Quality; required Engineering; optional autoresearch; a reusable A2A Adapter; no second scheduler or universal workflow DSL. A new reusable capability implementation may still require deployment.
  • After the narrowed spikes and resource review: Kestra OSS v2.0.3 is the observed behavioral development baseline, not a selected product runtime. Its ~650 MiB warm-idle JVM RSS excludes PostgreSQL and Strands; a separate Kestra/database pair per harness is rejected as the default. A shared local pair requires a measured whole-install envelope. Dagu, non-development Temporal and core Strands Graph have bounded countertrials.

The revised logical arrangement is:

Customized Strands harness
  Director agent: understands the brief and requests authorized decisions
  Factory Module: publication, invocation, status, decisions, cancellation
  A2A Interface: exposes this harness's factory capability
  Adapter/reconciliation: connects durable engine work and remote tasks
  Durable workflow execution and storage supplied by the installation
    Embedded runtime or automatically managed bundled local helpers
    Native definitions, scheduling, waits, retries and execution history
       |
Agent capabilities, including other factory-enabled Strands harnesses

Durable product records + artifact storage are part of the runtime package.
Quality/Engineering are responsibilities, not mandatory extra processes.

The Factory Module should provide Depth through a small Interface: publishing an allowed composition, starting work, inspecting its evidence, submitting a scoped decision, and requesting cancellation. These are proposed operations, not an SDK specification. Implementation details such as engine task identities, callback delivery and reconciliation belong inside the Module. Engine-specific operations stay in an Adapter; do not build a general engine abstraction before the comparative slice shows an actual need.

The Director's conversation is not the execution ledger. Harness restart or conversation compaction must not create new work accidentally. A durable current-owner check must reject commands from a superseded Director instance. Routine deterministic progress should not require an LLM call at each graph edge. The Director is invoked for the decisions the factory policy assigns to it. Locally durable state must survive process restart; surviving loss of the entire host additionally requires backup/replication, which is an explicit production decision. Self-contained orchestration still permits configured model providers and remote A2A capabilities.

The initial trust assumption is trusted local harness code and configured capabilities. Application Interfaces still enforce scoped commands, current ownership and independent Quality acceptance. Separate identities and state prevent operational collisions; they do not establish protection against hostile code running as the same OS user or hard CPU/memory isolation. Those stronger boundaries are unqualified and deferred. S2/S4 check the supported application paths; they do not become sandbox or arbitrary-code containment projects. Revisit containment only when a concrete requirement or observed failure makes it necessary.

New source evidence that changes the spike order

> Follow-up, 22 September 2026: the Conductor package-rights investigation subsequently built a PostgreSQL-only source variant without the direct restricted dependency and ran a simple workflow across restart. The stock artifact remains uncleared; reproducible product packaging, full notices and S1–S4 factory behavior remain open. The hypothesis below records the original spike-plan state.

Artifact eligibility is also unresolved for a concrete reason. The v3.32.4 server declares io.orkes.queues:orkes-conductor-queues, pinned to 2.0.0.rc3. Its published POM declares the Orkes Community License, whose Article 3.3 contains third-party-service and competitive-product restrictions. This is not the Apache core license. The intended assembled product therefore needs explicit clearance or removal of that dependency; it is not established as a permitted baseline merely by building the repository. Server declaration, dependency version, published POM, pinned license.

The dependency also appears through other modules. Selecting PostgreSQL at runtime does not remove it from the stock package. At planning time, a PostgreSQL-only assembly excluding the restricted dependency and dependent modules was an uncompiled hypothesis. The later follow-up established a narrow source-build and restart path, not a distributable or factory-qualified product. This artifact restriction and the newly required self-contained operation both qualify the previous Conductor recommendation; its feature score remains documentation-based technical coverage, now adjusted for the omitted workflow event listener.

Conductor's PostgreSQL documentation describes persistence, queues, indexing and locking, while explicitly advising workload-specific benchmarking. That establishes a supported configuration claim, not our reliability or capacity result. PostgreSQL documentation.

The reviewed v3.32.4 lock source uses expiring database rows and thread-local holds. Its release/delete paths warrant tests involving lease expiry, failed acquisition and stale owners. The task-update path also warrants overlapping completion/cancellation tests: state checks and persistence are separate operations, and the ordinary update path does not itself demonstrate a compare-and-swap guard. These are source-grounded race hypotheses, not reproduced failures or a claim that Conductor is unusable. Pinned lock source, pinned execution source, PostgreSQL execution persistence.

The independent review proposed ZooKeeper as a possible fallback. Treat that as unverified for the pinned distribution: the source review did not establish a bundled ZooKeeper implementation in v3.32.4. A guide mentioning it is insufficient. Verify an actual available implementation before proposing it as a remedy; changing lock storage would not automatically fix a separate task-update race. Pinned deployment guide, server dependencies, module inventory.

Strands documents plugins and A2A serving, supporting the direction of a harness extension. Its current A2A documentation also distinguishes per-context agent construction from a shared agent instance; documents caller-supplied context IDs as insufficient access protection; and identifies limitations in the high-level client for structured interrupt replies. Pin the actual SDK and test the exact public Interface. A stock text-oriented wrapper is not automatically the required factory task contract. Plugins, A2A serving, contexts and interrupts.

Proposed spikes

S0 — Establish a permitted, self-contained runtime package

Question: can we supply factory operation with the harness installation, with no separately provisioned workflow platform and no required restricted commercial dependency?

Plan: first screen the candidate against the accepted native installation with automatically managed bundled helpers. Record source commit, dependency inventory, artifact digest, included server/UI/modules, licenses, configuration and intended delivery model. For a Conductor trial, use v3.32.4 as the reviewed starting candidate, not an assertion that it is the latest release. Resolve the restricted queue dependency through every dependency path. Assess installation, managed local storage, process lifecycle, ports, startup/shutdown, recovery, update/backup ownership and actual startup/idle memory and disk footprint. Bundled helpers must come under the harness launcher rather than require a user's separate server setup. In-process execution is not required. Evaluate JVM overhead through these observations, with no language-based disqualification and no sandbox implementation.

PostgreSQL persistence/queues/indexing with explicit locking remains a conditional topology to assess, not a settled choice for the self-contained harness. Inspect actual loaded providers and disable accidental in-memory/development substitutes. After dependencies are available, test start, execution and restart without a remote orchestrator, vendor-network access or vendor key. Locally bundled infrastructure remains reachable. A Docker-only path does not satisfy the native baseline; no optional container or sandbox backend needs evaluation now.

Pass: a documented permitted artifact, self-contained startup within the agreed footprint, an observable native workflow, durable restart and identified providers; no required external orchestration platform or paid-only facility without an accepted alternative. If local helpers are shared, start two independently launched harness agents, stop/restart the first launcher, and verify process lifetime, port/store ownership and surviving work. One agent exiting must not silently destroy another's runtime. A successful offline boot proves behavior only, not license permission.

Decision/stop: unresolved distribution rights, incompatible process requirements or missing mandatory runtime capabilities block that artifact. Missing native A2A does not block it if the agreed Adapter can supply the required contract. Record the cost of every alternative. Do not turn this into an engine-embedding or dependency-remediation project. Re-screen lighter local runtimes if the existing server-oriented candidates fail this gate.

Scope: one pinned baseline; no deployment automation, load benchmark or production approval. Supports the entry conditions in the existing evaluation.

S1 — Test the engine's contested state before building around it

Question: do locking, task updates and recovery converge correctly under the failures our product will create?

Plan: first use a tiny native workflow with deterministic tasks. Force overlapping updates, lock acquisition failure and lease overrun. Race completion against completion, timeout and cancellation. Kill/restart a process after persistence but before queue acknowledgement; interrupt storage access and restore it. Observe actual lock ownership, task history, downstream starts and reconciliation. If the proposed runtime permits multiple engine processes sharing a store, add the two-process lease case; otherwise prove exclusive store ownership and confine the first litmus to the supported local topology. Do not make distributed HA an accidental initial product requirement.

Pass: a coherent observable outcome under a race policy agreed before execution; no lost durable work, irreversible unauthorized progress, unexplained stuck join or corruption. Declare completion/cancellation/timeout precedence, the authoritative commit point and permitted downstream effects before observing results. At-least-once task delivery is allowed and must be measured; external effects still need their own idempotency. A duplicate delivery is not itself a failed engine test. A completion/cancellation race need not always choose cancellation, but an observed result cannot be used to invent its own passing policy.

Decision/stop: reproduce source suspicions before declaring defects. Separate configuration failure, lock-provider defect, engine-kernel defect and missing product fencing. Evaluate one bounded remedy on a verified available implementation. If reliable execution requires owning a substantial scheduler/kernel fork or serializing the entire platform externally, reconsider Conductor and move the same litmus to Kestra. A higher coverage score cannot excuse the failure.

Scope: correctness litmus, not HA certification. Run the early litmus immediately after S0; broader recovery tests can follow the harness fixture. Relates to E03/E05/E09 and M01/M03 without completing them.

S2 — Make a Strands harness act as a durable factory service

Question: can factory functionality live in the customized harness while durable progress and authority survive that harness?

Plan: add the smallest Factory Module to a pinned Strands setup. Configure one ordinary capability agent and one factory Director using the same harness package. Give each instance its own stable identity, state namespace, configuration and workspace, with collision-free endpoints. Expose the latter through an A2A factory contract, start one run, wait for a Director decision and restart the harness. Resume under the same instance identity from durable evidence; confirm the other instance's state is unchanged. Replace the Director's execution incarnation and deliver a stale command from the old incarnation. Invoke a child factory hosted by another instance of the same harness; test parent cancellation and child result retrieval. Shared storage is allowed with explicit per-instance ownership; no sandbox is needed for this lifecycle proof.

Pass: one installation supplies the capability agent, factory Director, durable execution and A2A endpoint; no separately provisioned workflow service or bespoke factory application per agent. Reconnecting or repeating a tool call does not duplicate an assignment. The current Director can inspect/resume the same run, and stale or unauthorized commands are rejected. Factory completion reflects accepted output, not merely the Director returning a chat response. Reused harness code supports both capability and factory roles without bespoke graph code per factory.

Decision/stop: if this requires replacing Strands' agent loop, turning its session memory into a scheduler, or constructing a separate bespoke factory host for every agent, revise the integration design before selecting the stack. Any proposed engine must satisfy S0's process/dependency requirement first.

Scope: one parent, one child, one wait and one restart; no elaborate Director prompt or UI. Stub model decisions initially to isolate lifecycle behavior, then schedule real-agent validation under Q1. Supports E02/E03/E09 and the newly accepted harness requirement.

S3 — Prove native publication and complete immutable bindings

Question: can agents publish useful factory documents without harness refresh, while active work keeps its intended semantics?

Plan: use the reference factory: two research branches, synthesis, independent review, one bounded repair path, Director wait and controlled delivery. Declare the supported native task/expression profile. Publish v1 and leave it waiting before a child/dynamic task starts; publish v2 and alter aliases or attempt same-version metadata mutation. Exercise child definitions, task definitions, retry settings, capability revisions, evaluation policy and dynamic selection. Try a schema-valid review bypass, an unapproved task type/destination and excessive fan-out.

Pass: new compositions run through the same harness/worker deployments. Accepted v1 dependency bindings stay fixed; v2 applies to new admissions. Mutation or undeclared resolution is rejected or made immutable by the publisher. Dangerous configurations cannot escape the supported profile, and errors are actionable. Emergency revocation may stop future dispatch without rewriting the recorded binding.

Decision/stop: explicit versioned task names, dependency manifests and restricted native constructs are plausible costs. Owning an arbitrary-code safety prover, universal compiler or custom workflow interpreter is a material architecture change. Count it as such. Do not require static proof of arbitrary expressions; constrain the language and enforce effect permissions at runtime as needed.

Scope: one useful native vocabulary and one new composition. Conductor snapshots some static metadata; do not assume every dependency is late-bound, or that a parent snapshot freezes everything reached later. Inspect actual behavior. Supports E01/M05/M07. Pinned metadata resolution.

S4 — Prove remote recovery and acceptance across transaction gaps

Question: can the harness's Adapter and product records safely connect remote task state, acceptance decisions and engine transitions?

Plan: reuse the reference factory with deterministic fixtures for a pinned A2A version/binding. Persist intent before dispatch. Drop a response after remote acceptance, including before recording its task ID. Duplicate and reorder observations; restart during input-required and authorization-required waits; deliver a stale attempt after its replacement. Exercise both a cooperative deduplicating receiver and a receiver without discovery/deduplication. Crash between product-decision commit, engine update and acknowledgement. Reject r1, produce r2, and race stale/duplicate approvals and conflicting Director commands. Lose the final delivery receipt separately.

Pass: cooperative services yield one logical effect; unsupported guarantees yield an explicit unknown outcome and no unsafe automatic resubmission. One current attempt and exact eligible artifact revision can advance acceptance. Accepted artifacts survive delivery recovery. Durable command identity and replay/reconciliation recover partial commits without a second scheduler. Transient projection lag is allowed; permanent contradictory authority or double effects are not. All exposed task/control Interfaces enforce actor scope; raw engine administration is outside ordinary agent authority. This proves application authorization under the stated local trust assumption, not containment of hostile same-user code.

Decision/stop: a small durable intent/outbox/inbox and reconciliation implementation is plausible common product work, not a Conductor-specific defect. Sharing a PostgreSQL server does not make HTTP engine updates and product transactions atomic. If the design needs competing authoritative run state or a second dispatch engine, redesign it and reassess total ownership. A remote service without safe redispatch is a service-contract limitation; changing engines does not fix it.

Scope: selected failure windows with exact call counts, not every protocol transport. Verify artifacts are durable, readable and digest-bound before acceptance; the full storage/security qualification follows under Q1/Q3. Covers selected E03–E09 cases.

S5 — Prove bounded authority, maintenance and improvement

Question: can the same harness functionality support our governance and Engineering model without privileged agent shortcuts?

Plan: contend for the final synthetic budget reservation across two branches and a nested factory. Duplicate/delay usage and cancel work whose remote outcome is unknown. Have two observers claim one incident, replace its owner, apply one approved remedy and exhaust its retry limit. With autoresearch disabled, submit one trace-derived improvement, independently evaluate it, and publish v2 through S3. Race promotions and attempt author self-approval, evaluator modification and use of unauthorized credentials. Plan one external-watcher restart/escalation check for an unavailable engine.

Pass: spend is attributed once at the agreed charge owner; unresolved remote exposure is retained rather than released just because a local lease expires. One current recovery owner acts within bounds and closes an incident only on observed recovery. Quality controls acceptance independently of the candidate author. Promotion checks the expected current version, preserves active bindings and can roll back future admissions. Disabled autoresearch leaves maintenance and ordinary improvement functional. The watcher does not schedule factory tasks.

Decision/stop: enforceable ceilings require cooperating services or defensible upper bounds. Fixture success cannot establish a strict cap at an arbitrary provider. If a supported Director command permits self-approval or protected evaluator changes, fix the application authority boundary before claiming governance. Arbitrary shell access under a trusted local account is outside this proof; do not expand it into sandbox work. If ordinary remediation requires continuous free-form replanning, the claimed small recovery Module needs reassessment.

Scope and staging: the engine-choice portion is limited to three small proofs through the existing reference slice: reject self-approval/evaluator mutation; fence one stale recovery owner; and admit one independently approved new version with research disabled. Give each an explicit effort/stop budget before execution. The budget-collision, full remediation, watcher, promotion-race and rollout/rollback extensions become Q2/Q3 implementation qualification unless an earlier result makes them decisive for engine choice. Reuse synthetic decisions; no autonomous campaign or statistical benchmark. Supports selected E10/M01–M08 obligations, without claiming full scenario passes or requiring the whole platform before choosing an engine.

S6 — Give Kestra a fair chance to overturn the preference

Question: among candidates that meet self-contained deployment, does Conductor actually reduce total owned work compared with the closest viable alternative?

Plan: Kestra is the proposed countertrial only if it also clears S0. Otherwise choose a candidate with a credible accepted local deployment and update this plan together first. Preserve the harness's public factory contract, fixtures and acceptance policy. Express the reference factory in that runtime's native definition and assess parallel remote waits, one restart, nested invocation, v1/v2 publication and the failed-state diagnosis path. Credit a reusable Adapter equally. Test only equivalent slices already understood on Conductor; do not repeat the full audit of every engine.

Authoring comparison: proposed small sample of six matched tasks: create, add a parallel branch, add bounded repair, nest a factory, correct a mapping error, and reject a forbidden bypass. Use the same author model, tool budget, documentation access and three independent attempts per task/engine. Record semantic success, unsafe acceptance, repair turns, token/tool cost and human intervention. This is a directional comparison, not a benchmark proving that a DSL is universally best for agents. Paid model use and the actual budget remain to be agreed.

Pass/decision: both must satisfy the selected invariants; rank implementation burden and operation afterward. Choose Kestra if it provides comparable correct behavior with materially simpler integration or more usable authoring/diagnosis. Prefer Conductor if its task model clearly reduces that burden and S1's concerns are resolved. Record durable state, recovery paths, upgrades, custom plugins and deployment units, not just lines of code. A small inconclusive authoring sample does not overrule correctness evidence.

Scope: a focused countertrial. Reassess a maintained authoring layer under the accepted automatic-rollout model: preserve active versions, automate publication, and measure retained-worker cost. Zigflow’s observed refresh behavior alone is no longer a rejection. Argo/Dagu receive further trials only if evidence or deployment requirements make them plausible winners. No excluded product distribution is silently reinstated.

Complete planning assumption register

This register covers the material assumptions visible in the current architecture. Accepted means a product requirement, not verified implementation. Documented means source/documentation support, not local runtime proof. Hypothesis requires experimental evidence. Open requires a product or deployment choice. A spike cannot choose a product policy merely by producing a successful demo.

What should follow selection, rather than delay all development

Q1 — Real-service and harness validation. Run the chosen slice against at least one real Strands-hosted capability and an independently implemented A2A peer. Verify the pinned wire contract, meaningful outputs, structured continuation, scoped artifacts, model/provider provenance, context isolation and actual cost limits. Authorize provider usage and agree budget first. A deterministic fixture cannot prove model quality, real interoperability or remote spend enforcement. No complete claim of factory service compatibility precedes this work.

Q2 — Full Engineering and optional research qualification. Implement and validate the remaining required M01–M08 cases, including successor-run recovery and protected evaluation with research disabled. Agree quality metrics before claiming improvement. Qualify R01–R05 only before enabling autoresearch. Do not remove required maintenance/improvement from the product merely because the first decision spike exercises only one case.

Q3 — Production operation. Define workload/SLOs; qualify realistic throughput, long waits/outages, storage-failure handling, backup restoration, queue/history/artifact retention, upgrades, credential rotation and full authorization coverage. Database failover is required only if the selected topology promises it. Establish loss and recovery objectives and prove them on the actual topology. Complete full E01–E10 and relevant M coverage before corresponding production claims. Multi-customer shared-engine qualification is conditional on adding that deployment model.

The first implementation should grow from the reusable harness extension, native reference definition and evidence fixture. Defer a catalog marketplace, universal engine wrapper, elaborate board, arbitrary code-generation pipeline and autonomous optimization system. Sandbox research, sandbox backends and whole-harness containment are also deferred until a concrete blocker; they are not automatic follow-up gates for engine choice or first development. Per-instance identity/state, application authorization and durable recovery remain required. The factory's shared Interface and invariants come first.

Original parallel plan and executed narrowing

The owner approved the necessary first round and explicitly deferred S5, broad S6 and sandbox work. Parallel agents ran isolated S0, S2 and S3 work while S1/S4 used their own candidate instances and product fixtures. The result report is the authority for what actually ran; the steps below retain the original planning logic and broader future scope.

  1. Agree spike scope, unanswered product choices, pinned stack, pass/fail criteria, timeboxes and any model-spend budget. Done for the narrowed S0–S4 development probes only; production budgets and thresholds remain open.
  2. Establish a shared test contract: identity scheme, synthetic capability/result schemas, independent-review policy, evidence format and fault-controller conventions. Publish the fixture revision before dependent agents use it.
  3. Wave A: one subagent owns S0 then the early S1 litmus; another prepares S2's harness contract and fixture in isolation. Its engine integration depends on S0. A third may prepare S3 definitions/policy cases against the agreed fixture. Source/schema work can proceed before the runtime baseline; runtime conclusions require it. Stop candidate-specific investment if it fails the self-contained deployment gate.
  4. Wave B: after the baseline and harness contract stabilize, run S3 publication, S4 lifecycle/transactions and S5 bounded authority in parallel. Give each its own databases, queues, ports, run IDs and output directory; share immutable fixtures, not live state. S4/S5 must agree the acceptance/ownership Interface before implementation splits.
  5. Wave C: the broad S6 countertrial is deferred. Kestra became the observed candidate after the Conductor stock package gate stopped its runtime work. An independent evidence audit checked provenance and limits; reproduce decisive failures independently before an engine selection.
  6. Review results together. Record an engine decision only after required choice gates pass and custom ownership is acceptable. An inconclusive or blocked experiment does not count as success. Preserve rejected alternatives and the conditions that would reopen them.

The concurrency plan describes logical lanes, not a requirement for a fixed number of agents. Dependencies stay sequential even when workers are available. Agents must not silently modify the shared requirements to make their implementation pass.

Every result should record candidate/source/image/SDK/fixture digests, enabled providers, configuration, test hypothesis, actual concurrency and repetitions, injected failure point, expected/observed events, retained evidence and remaining uncertainty. Proposed initial fixtures remain ten concurrent factory runs with two branches, and twenty deliberately overlapping duplicate requests. These numbers are reproducibility settings, not an accepted production capacity target. Agree repetition counts and stop budgets before running contested cases.

Open questions to settle together
  1. Packaging envelope: bundled local helpers and the simple native baseline are settled. What initial platforms, other prerequisites and idle/startup footprint are acceptable? Recommendation: no manual database/server setup; measure one local runtime shared by agents in an installation. Docker/sandbox qualification is outside the current plan. No numerical limit has been set; Java/JVM remains eligible.
  2. First factory: identify the first useful outcome and allowed effects. Recommendation: use verified research as the repeatable fixture, then substitute the actual first customer workflow before Q1.
  3. Quality independence: define the required separation. Recommendation: separately authorized reviewer identity/context with protected evaluation and no author self-approval; different model/provider only where the quality requirement warrants it.
  4. Director automation: define actions allowed automatically and escalation limits. Recommendation: routine commands inside a fixed delegated scope; protected permission/evaluator/budget-policy changes require independent authority.
  5. Cost promise: strict provider-enforced ceiling or bounded admission with explicit uncertain exposure? Recommendation: hard limits only for cooperating providers; otherwise expose uncertainty and stop unsafe new admissions.
  6. Concrete stack and operations: identify an existing customized harness, if any; choose SDK/language/protocol from its actual support; decide packaged/self-hosted delivery versus operated hosting. Recommendation: one initial stack and one organization's deployment, without promising future shared-engine isolation prematurely.
  7. Evaluation budget: agree per-spike effort limits, model-call allowance, workload envelope and decision deadline. Recommendation: fail fast on S0/S1/S2, reuse one fixture, and expand comparative work only when it could change the choice.

Reference comparison / decision-round product trials

Keep the tradeoffs visible.
Close the product proof gates.

The decision-round comparison ranked Dagu narrowly ahead of Effect for development at that stage, with Strands Graph third. A fresh 23 September review instead recommends Temporal first, Effect second, and Dagu third for development. Dagu's native YAML and nested DAGs simplify agent-authored composition; Effect's durable replay has the stronger acceptance-gap evidence. Both ran copied local supervisors with two Director harnesses, but clean-machine installation, distribution and complete real-service behavior remain unqualified. The feature matrix below is historical source coverage, not this product judgment.

DEVELOPMENT CHOICE · CONDITIONAL
01 / Conductor

Prove OSS suitability and the A2A contract.

Its native factory documents fit service composition. First prove that the OSS distribution and access boundary meet our needs; then test recovery, continuation and factory-as-A2A exposure through the chosen integration. Native A2A completeness is not required.

A2A integration ↗ · Native definitions ↗

02 / Kestra

Compare authoring and operational effort.

Use the same capability contracts in native YAML and measure one shared local engine across multiple harnesses. Its authoring resources are compelling; the ~650 MiB warm-idle JVM and Basic Auth boundary make the complete package a decisive gate.

Authoring resources ↗ · A2A task contract ↗

03 / Temporal

A viable reliability comparator.

One stable Python interpreter on non-development Server 1.32.0 published v2 while v1 waited and recovered both after server, worker and PostgreSQL restart. This clears the Zigflow-specific rollout concern; own the document language and measure the complete local process set.

Round-two result ↗
04 / Argo Workflows

Prove the Kubernetes tradeoff.

Use approved versioned templates and scoped service accounts. Run the same nested waits, recovery and artifact gates; measure controller/pod overhead and the work required by the A2A adapter. A mutable template name is not a version binding.

05 / Dagu product trial

Native YAML; bind every child.

Community v2.17.0 passed pinned root-and-child publication, Strands/A2A assignments, exact artifact acceptance and copied local supervisor recovery. Its shared two-Director trial used about 676 MiB summed waiting RSS. Host-unique run IDs, explicit post-acceptance retry, atomic publication, in-flight Director fencing and GPL-compliant distribution remain product work.

Decision-round result ↗ · Bundle review ↗

06 / Strands Graph

Direct harness fit; own the run boundary.

Graph 1.57.0 restored pinned sessions and a Strands Director's A2A task after a hard stop. The product still owns definition publication, scheduling, remote reconciliation, acceptance and delivery fencing. A forced lease expiry sent twice; the synthetic receiver accepted one action by its own stable key. Its two parallel assignments were not joined into a meaningful reviewed result.

Graph SDK ↗ · Decision-round result ↗

07 / Effect Workflow

Durable replay; build the graph language.

Effect's SQL-backed helper recovered remote uncertainty, acceptance-signal crashes and a copied local supervisor hard stop. Two Directors shared one helper at about 674 MiB summed waiting RSS. The current definition interpreter accepts only two fixed linear shapes; flexible approved graphs and nested factories need product code.

A director wait handles missing input or exhausted repair. Acceptance records the exact artifact revision. Test nesting through both native composition and the factory’s public A2A contract.

Decisive proof / ten reproducible scenarios

Author and publish. Validate native definitions, reject a review bypass, publish a new composition without worker deployment, and retain v1 bindings while v2 is introduced.

Recover remote work. Restart during work or input-required waits. Lose the acceptance response, race duplicate submissions, and distinguish a known task from an unknown remote outcome.

Protect accepted evidence. Reject malformed outputs, unreadable artifacts, stale attempts, and obsolete approvals. A repair produces a new revision with its own required review.

Recover the failed stage. Keep successful research during branch recovery. Retain accepted artifacts when delivery fails, and reconcile a missing publication receipt.

Control nested work. Test authorized director commands, conflicting responses, cancellation races, and actual child outcomes. Nested invocation is required; self-recursion is optional.

Bound concurrent starts. Proposed fixture settings: ten simultaneous runs, two research branches each, and twenty duplicate submissions. Exercise shared capacity and cooperative budget reservations.

Lifecycle coverage is now part of the baseline. The same proof includes incident ownership, bounded remediation, safe candidate evaluation, and version promotion. Proactive research is tested only when enabled; a disabled lab does not remove maintenance or process engineering.

Choose by proven behavior and custom integration cost. Record what the engine supplies, what Exomachina adds, and what the remote service guarantees. Candidate roles set the evaluation scope; weighted coverage helps prioritize proof. All eight options remain comparable. Dagu has no score until a complete assessment; Strands Graph has no comparable operational score until its complete product path is assessed; change the shortlist only when evidence or requirements warrant it. Missing required behavior stays visible regardless of score.

Use deterministic agent fixtures for repeatable fault tests, followed by real-service interoperability checks. The plan shares contracts and evidence while retaining each engine’s native workflow language. Full reference-factory and production results remain unrun; the separate Temporal/Zigflow development probes are recorded in the focused evaluation. Add required maintenance scenarios M01–M08 and optional research scenarios R01–R05 from the component specification.

01

Protocol & capability bindings

Choose an A2A version and transport, verify the native integration or reusable adapter, and define contract versioning and compatibility checks.

02

Service administration & authority

Keep harness, provider, model, reasoning, and fallback policy in service administration. Define advertised guarantees and who may publish or invoke each capability.

03

Task identity & recovery

Design the mapping from factory runs and assignments to attempts and A2A tasks. Prove recovery and duplicate handling under concurrent requests; see the lifecycle design agenda.

04

Artifacts & context isolation

Choose durable artifact storage, lineage, revision-bound acceptance, retention, and cleanup order. Keep factual memory, procedural skills, and execution truth separate.

05

Publication & version policy

Define supported primitives, complete dependency bindings, gate policy, limits, automatic approval scope, and immutable publication evidence. Learnings propose new versions; they do not rewrite active runs.

06

Hosting & operational ownership

Verify pinned releases and compare the complete one-install idle/paused/active memory, startup, disk, process ownership, paid-feature dependencies, capacity, budgets and upgrades.

07

Maintenance coverage & self-healing

Bind Engineering and the current recovery owner, incident identity, approved remedies, recovery limits, independent watcher, and escalation route. Define observed evidence of restored health.

08

Improvement & optional research

Define protected evaluators, candidate lineage, promotion and rollout rules, and rejection history. An optional research charter adds an editable surface, finite campaign budgets, and isolated capacity.

Agents provide the capabilities.
Factories define the cooperation.
